# Evidence

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/evidence/


A ticket travels as an evidence bundle: the signed facts, the hash-pinned
rules that judge them, the registry the signatures check against, and a
script that checks the lot with coreutils. Whoever holds one recomputes
the answer.

That is the whole claim, and it is a narrow one. A build system tells you
a process ran. A bundle tells you *which* rules judged it, what they
required, what was supplied, and lets you recompute the verdict on a
laptop with no network, years later.

- [Bundle format](/evidence/bundle-format/) — the on-disk contract, what
  a reader may assume, and what forces a version bump.
- [Re-deriving a bundle](/evidence/re-deriving/) — `tik rederive`, the
  HTTP service, and what a badge is allowed to say.
- [SLSA, said honestly](/evidence/slsa/) — what the release processes
  demand, mapped onto SLSA's requirements, and where that mapping stops.

## What a bundle is worth

A guard checks that a trusted attester said something. It never reads the
SBOM. So a derivation is exactly as good as the attesters named in it,
and that belongs in the first paragraph rather than a footnote — the
signatures prove *who claimed*, the hashes prove *what was claimed*, and
the definition proves *which rule accepted it*.

What the format adds on top of a signed archive is the rules. Two people
holding the same bundle reach the same stages, because the definition
that judged the ticket travels inside it, addressed by its own hash.


---

# Bundle format

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/evidence/bundle-format/


`tik-evidence-bundle`, version 1. A gzipped tar holding one ticket and
everything its derivation needs.

```sh
tik bundle <id> --out evidence.tgz
```

```text
bundle.edn                          the format name and version
actors                              the allowed-signers registry
pq-signers                          the ML-DSA-65 key registry, where the store keeps one
signatures.edn                      the signature policy, where the store sets one
roles.edn                           role membership, where the store keeps a register
delegation.edn                      the store's delegation policy, where it sets one
identity/<event-id>.edn             key bindings and delegations, as signed registry events
identity/<event-id>.sig.<fpr>       their authorship signatures
identity/keys/<kid>.pem             the issuer keys those bindings rest on
processes/by-hash/<hash>.edn        the definition the ticket pinned
processes/by-hash/<hash>.sig.<fpr>  its publication signatures
tickets/<uuid>/events/<id>.edn      the append-only log
tickets/<uuid>/events/<id>.sig.<fpr>      authorship signatures
tickets/<uuid>/events/<id>.pqsig.<fpr>    post-quantum authorship signatures
tickets/<uuid>/events/<id>.witness.<fpr>  countersignatures over a head
tickets/<uuid>/events/<id>.pqwitness.<fpr>  ML-DSA-65 countersignatures sealing an ancestry
tickets/<uuid>/blobs/<hash>         attached artifacts, addressed by content
verify.sh                           a coreutils implementation of the checks
README.md                           what the recipient is holding
```

## What a reader may assume

**Every stored file's name is the SHA-256 of its bytes**, prefixed
`sha256-`. Event and definition files carry a `.edn` suffix after the
address; blobs are named by the bare address. `sha256sum` alone audits
the archive.

**Event bytes are exactly the hashed region.** An event file holds the
canonical serialization *without* its `:event/id`, because the filename
is the id. Re-emitting a parsed event reproduces the file byte for byte.

**Signatures are detached siblings.** `<id>.sig.<fingerprint>` covers the
event's stored bytes under the `tik-event` namespace; `<id>.witness.<fpr>`
covers a head under `tik-witness`; a definition's `.sig.<fpr>` uses
`tik-process`. Each verifies with `ssh-keygen -Y verify` against
`actors`. `<id>.pqsig.<fpr>` is the raw FIPS 204 ML-DSA-65 signature over
the bytes `tik-event-v1`, a NUL byte, then the event's stored bytes, by
the `pq-signers` key whose DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo hashes (SHA-256, hex)
to `<fpr>`.

**Exactly one ticket directory, with exactly one root event.** Every
parent an event names is present in the same directory, so the Merkle DAG
the log commits to is complete.

**The pinned definition travels.** The create event carries
`:ticket/process-hash`, and `processes/by-hash/<that hash>.edn` holds the
definition whose content address equals it.

**`identity/` holds excerpts.** A key binding travels as the single
registry event that made it, with its own authorship signature and the
issuer's public key. Its parents live in a registry ticket that stays
behind, so its standing rests on its content address plus the issuer's
signature over the id-token it carries.

**Delegations travel with the verdicts they cover.** A verdict signed by
the throwaway key of a `tik review --batch` (ADR 0037) counts only
through the delegation that names the key, so the bundle carries every
delegation covering one of its events, and `delegation.edn`
(`{:require-touch true}` or `false`) when the store sets a delegation
policy. A bundle without `delegation.edn` credits delegations without a
touch requirement, as a store without a policy does.

**The role register travels where the store keeps one.** `roles.edn`
maps each role to its members in the shape a definition declares,
`{:role {:members ["actor" …]} …}`, and replaces the definition's
members role by role. A bundle without `roles.edn` re-derives under the
definition's members, as a store without a register does. A `roles.edn`
that is present and does not parse, does not have that shape, or is not
a regular file makes the bundle unreadable: a reader refuses it rather
than fall back to the definition's members, because the register is how
a member's departure is expressed. The file carries no content address
and no signature, so it states the membership the producing store held
without proving it.

**`bundle.edn` declares the packaging version and nothing else.** The
ticket, the head, the definition and the stage are derivable from the
files, so the manifest names none of them and nothing in it is trusted.
A bundle without a manifest is version 1.

## The checks

These are what the format promises. `verify.sh` implements them with
coreutils, `ssh-keygen` and — for key bindings — `openssl`;
[`tik rederive`](/evidence/re-deriving/) implements them in process. The
script travels inside the archive it checks, so read it before you run
it, or run this list yourself.

1. **Integrity.** Every `tickets/*/events/*.edn`, `identity/*.edn`,
   `processes/by-hash/*.edn` and `tickets/*/blobs/*` hashes to its own
   name.
2. **Shape.** Exactly one ticket directory.
3. **Completeness.** Every parent referenced by an event is present, and
   exactly one event has empty `:event/parents`.
4. **Authorship.** Every `.sig.` sidecar verifies *as the actor its own
   event names* — binding `-I` to `:event/actor` rather than accepting
   whoever happened to sign, so a registered actor cannot sign another's
   authorship.
   Every `.pqsig.` sidecar likewise verifies as its event's actor through
   a `pq-signers` line that allows the `tik-event` namespace. A
   `.pqsig.` sidecar without `pq-signers` fails, and `verify.sh` fails
   one it cannot check because the host's OpenSSL is older than 3.5.
   A `.sig.` sidecar whose key `actors` does not grant still counts when
   a delegation in `identity/` covers it:
   - the delegation is an attestation by the event's actor, verifying
     through an `actors` line no key binding earned, and touched where
     `delegation.edn` requires it;
   - its window is at most five minutes and holds the event's
     `:event/at`;
   - its scope names the event's ticket together with one of the event's
     parents;
   - its facts name the path the event asserts;
   - the sidecar verifies against the key the delegation names.
5. **Countersignature.** Every `.witness.` sidecar verifies as a
   registered principal under `tik-witness`. Every `.pqwitness.` sidecar
   is an ML-DSA-65 signature over `tik-witness-v1\0` followed by the
   event's bytes, by a `pq-signers` key allowed `tik-witness`.
6. **Signature policy.** Where `signatures.edn` travels, it reads as
   `{:require #{:ssh-ed25519 …} :from <instant>}` over the algorithms
   `:ssh-ed25519` and `:ml-dsa-65`, or the bundle fails. Every event
   carries a verifying `ssh-ed25519` signature by its actor; from `:from`
   on, also one for every other required algorithm; and where
   `:ml-dsa-65` is required, every event claimed before `:from` is a
   `.pqwitness.` event or one of its ancestors.
7. **Key bindings.** For each binding in `identity/`: the issuer signed
   the id-token, using the key at `identity/keys/<kid>.pem`; the token's
   `sub` and `iss` equal the binding's; the token was live at the
   binding's `:event/at`; the token names the key it binds, as a `nonce`
   or an `aud` suffix equal to `tik-key-<sha256 of the key>` (ADR 0035);
   and the key it binds appears in `actors`.

Check 7 is checkable offline because the issuer's key travels in the
archive, and it says exactly this much: *whoever built this bundle holds
a token that this key signed, for this subject and this bound key, at
that moment.*
Recognizing the key as the issuer's is the reader's job, the same way
recognizing an `actors` line is — a subject like
`repo:metio/tik:ref:refs/heads/main` is worth what the reader knows about
that repository and that IdP.

An unsigned event is authenticity unclaimed rather than a failure, and a
binding whose issuer key is absent grants nothing and is reported as
such. Everything else in the list is a failure.

Deriving the ticket's stages needs the definition as well, which is where
`tik rederive` goes on and `verify.sh` stops.

## Compatibility

Version 1 is the layout above. The rules below are what a reader written
against it may rely on.

**A reader ignores what it does not recognize.** Unknown files,
directories and manifest keys are passed over. That is what makes the
additions in the next paragraph safe.

**These may appear without a version bump:**

- new top-level files and directories;
- new files inside existing directories, including new sidecar kinds
  (`<id>.<kind>.<fingerprint>`);
- new keys in `bundle.edn`;
- new event types, fact paths, guard operators and process keys inside
  the files, which are versioned by the kernel's own vocabularies rather
  than by this format;
- any change to `verify.sh` and `README.md`, which carry no contract of
  their own.

**These force a version bump:**

- moving, renaming or removing anything the layout names;
- changing what a name means — a different hash function, a different
  suffix convention, a signature namespace;
- changing the canonical serialization, which changes every event id and
  is versioned separately by `tik.canonical/format-version`;
- carrying more than one ticket;
- anything else that makes a conforming version-1 reader compute a
  different answer or fail.

A reader holding a bundle whose major version it does not know declines
it and says so.

## Reading a bundle yourself

The archive unpacks to plain files, so an implementation in any language
is a hash, a signature check and an EDN reader.

```sh
mkdir bundle && tar xzf evidence.tgz -C bundle && cd bundle

# 1. integrity, without any tool of ours
sha256sum tickets/*/events/*.edn | while read sum f; do
  [ "sha256-$sum" = "$(basename "$f" .edn)" ] || echo "MISMATCH $f"
done

# 2. authorship, as the actor each event names
for sig in tickets/*/events/*.sig.*; do
  ev="${sig%%.sig.*}.edn"
  actor=$(sed -n 's/^{:event\/actor "\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$ev")
  ssh-keygen -Y verify -f actors -I "$actor" -n tik-event -s "$sig" < "$ev"
done
```

Canonical bytes sort map keys, so `:event/actor` always leads an event
file — which is why one `sed` finds it.

## Relationship to in-toto

[in-toto](https://in-toto.io/) attestations describe a build: this
subject, this predicate, signed by this functionary. A bundle carries a
different kind of thing — the facts, the rules that judge them, and the
means to recompute the verdict offline. in-toto's nearest analogue is the
layout, and a tik process definition already is one.

The two compose. `tik bridge intoto` reads a SLSA provenance, an SPDX or
CycloneDX SBOM, or a vulnerability report into an attestation event, so
an `:attested-within` guard is satisfied by the format your pipeline
already emits, and the result travels in a bundle.


---

# Re-deriving a bundle

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/evidence/re-deriving/


`verify.sh` answers one question: are these bytes what they claim to be?
`tik rederive` answers the other one: what do they add up to?

```sh
tik rederive evidence.tgz
```

```text
bundle sha256-04a0bf413895fefb1c20e9231632fbc0d0a0d768275b42c097581ed19365973a
  format    tik-evidence-bundle version 1
  ticket    e26a1d57-6643-4564-99fa-8968ced7afa5  "2026.8.6132954"
  events    10
  judged by release sha256-3c577f361a46ec2166b7f4d6fb875d2de4e317f478d425eb4ae39f77fdcb9aca

verification
  ok   … hashes to its name and is schema-valid
  ok   every referenced parent is present
  ok   exactly one root event
  ok   … verifies as ci
  ok   ci is bound to its key by repo:metio/tik:ref:refs/heads/main, per …
  => the bytes are what they claim to be

derivation at 2026-08-06T20:29:26.198Z
  reached   :attested, :built, :scanned
  current   :attested, :scanned
  :built
      ✓ [:fact [:version]]
      ✓ [:signed-by :ci [:commit]]
      ✓ [:artifact "checksums/"]
  :scanned
      ✓ [:attested-within :vulnerability-scan "P1D"]
```

It takes a `.tgz`, an unpacked directory, or an `https` URL, and exits 1
when the bundle fails to verify — a derivation over bytes that are not
what they claim to be is worth nothing. `--edn` prints the same result as
data.

A bundle whose `roles.edn` is present but does not read as a role
register is refused with exit 1 and nothing derived from it; the service
answers such a bundle with status 400. Without `roles.edn`, the
definition's members stand (see [Bundle format](/evidence/bundle-format/)).

## Derivation names its instant

`reached` above is what the pinned rules grant **at the instant printed
under it**. The release process demands a vulnerability scan attested
within a day; a month from now the same archive, byte for byte, derives
`:built` alone — the scan it carries is real, signed, and too old for the
rule that reads it.

That is the reason to re-derive rather than record. A stored "passed"
survives its own evidence; a derivation ages with it.

## Gating on a bundle

Three flags turn re-derivation into a check a consumer's own CI can stand on:

```sh
tik rederive https://example.com/evidence.tgz \
  --expect-stage :published \
  --expect-definition sha256-3c577f361a46ec2166b7f4d6fb875d2de4e317f478d425eb4ae39f77fdcb9aca
```

Exit 0 when every named stage is reached under that exact definition, 1
otherwise, with a line saying which expectation failed and what was
derived instead.

**Pin the definition.** A bundle carries the rules that judged it, so a
supplier who writes those rules can reach any stage they choose —
`:published` becomes a claim about a process only once the reader names
*which* process. That is why `--expect-definition` takes the full hash
and refuses an abbreviation: eight hex characters is thirty-two bits for
somebody to collide with deliberately, and the value is pasted into a
workflow file once.

**Name who may bind a key.** A key the bundle earned through an identity
binding was accepted under the supplier's binding policy and checked
against issuer keys the supplier shipped, and the supplier chose both. A
token signed by a key the supplier made up can name any issuer and
subject. `--expect-bindings` applies your policy and your keys instead.
The policy has the shape `oidc.edn` uses:

```clojure
{:bindings {"ci" [{:issuer "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
                   :subject "repo:supplier/proj:ref:refs/heads/main"}]}}
```

```sh
tik rederive evidence.tgz --expect-bindings reader-oidc.edn
```

The issuer keys are read from `jwks/` beside that file, the layout a tik
store root already has, so a reader who runs tik points at their own
`oidc.edn` and pins issuers with `tik bridge jwks`. Every bound key must
then come from an issuer and subject your file permits for that actor,
with a token a key you pinned for that issuer signed. A subject ending in
`*` admits every subject that starts with what precedes it. A bundle whose signers are all listed in
its `actors` file passes and says that no signer rests on a binding. A
file without `:bindings`, or one that does not parse, is refused: a
policy that says nothing would pass every bundle.

## In GitHub Actions

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read
steps:
  - uses: metio/tik/.github/actions/install@2026.8.7062815
  - uses: metio/tik/.github/actions/verify@2026.8.7062815
    with:
      bundle: https://github.com/you/proj/releases/download/v1/evidence.tgz
      expect-stage: ":published"
      expect-definition: "sha256-3c577f36…"
```

The ref you pin *is* the tik you get: with no `version` input, the
installer resolves the release matching its own ref, so a pinned action
and a pinned tool are one decision rather than two.

The installer verifies before it trusts. It fetches the release's
`SHA256SUMS`, checks the cosign keyless signature naming the release
workflow that produced it, and only then checks the binary against those
checksums — an installer for a verification tool has no business asking
you to trust an unverified download. Linux/amd64 gets the native binary;
other platforms get the portable jar and need a JDK already on PATH.

`verify` needs `tik` on PATH and does one thing with it, so bring your
own build if you have one.

## The service

```sh
tik rederive --serve --port 7788
```

```text
POST /rederive                     the bundle as the request body -> EDN
GET  /derivation?bundle=<url>      fetch it, re-derive, render the page
GET  /badge.svg?bundle=<url>       the same, as a badge
```

Every request re-derives. The one thing held between requests is a cache
keyed by the bundle's content address *and* the minute the answer was
computed for — both inputs to the derivation, both immutable, so an entry
is either exactly right or absent and the whole cache is disposable.

The service fetches `https` URLs whose every resolved address is public,
follows at most four redirects, checking each hop, and caps what it will
download. It runs nothing from inside a bundle: the `verify.sh` that
travels in an archive is a convenience for whoever chooses to run it, and
the service implements the checks itself.

Point a README badge at a release artifact:

```markdown
[![evidence](https://your-host/badge.svg?bundle=https://github.com/you/proj/releases/download/v1/evidence.tgz)](https://your-host/derivation?bundle=https://github.com/you/proj/releases/download/v1/evidence.tgz)
```

## What a badge says

The stages the pinned definition grants, and which definition granted
them: `release@3c577f36 · :attested · :scanned`. The badge links to a
page carrying the guards that held, the ones that did not, who may sign
in this bundle and on whose say-so, and the two commands that reach the
same answer with the service switched off.

A badge is a derived conclusion displayed as though it were a fact, which
is the one thing [derived beats
declared](/concepts/derived-beats-declared/) forbids storing. Three
properties keep it honest:

- **it is derived per request**, so it is a lens rather than a status;
- **it names the derivation** — stages, definition hash, instant — where
  a word like *compliant* would name a policy it cannot see;
- **the service is disposable.** Delete it and the bundle still checks
  out with coreutils. A verification service that becomes the authority
  has re-introduced exactly the trust the bundle removes.

The colour follows the same rule: one shade for a bundle that verifies,
red for one that does not. Green would read as approval, and the badge
reports a derivation, which is a different kind of claim.

## Publishing bundles from CI

The wedge is one line over evidence a pipeline already produces. tik's own
release workflow records the version, the commit, the image digest and
the checksums file as signed facts, imports the SBOM, provenance and scan
as attestations through `tik bridge intoto`, and ships the result:

```sh
tik bundle "$TICKET" --out "evidence-$VERSION.tgz"
```

CI signs with an ephemeral key bound to its workload identity ([ADR
0023](/decisions/0023-key-bindings-are-evidence/)), so the bundle carries
the binding and its issuer's key, and a recipient re-earns that trust from
the issuer's own signature.


---

# SLSA, said honestly

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/evidence/slsa/


The stages of [`supply-chain-release`](/processes/supply-chain-release/) and
[`automated-release`](/processes/automated-release/) are named after the
evidence they demand, never after a level
in a framework. That is deliberate. tik checks that a **trusted attester said**
a thing; it never reads an SBOM or a provenance document and forms no opinion
about their contents. A stage called `slsa-l3` would put that overclaim into
the derivation itself, where every badge, lens and consumer assertion would
faithfully repeat it.

What `supply-chain-release` demands maps onto SLSA's build requirements like
this — and the table is a claim about **the definition**, never about any
ticket that pins it. `automated-release` demands the same, minus the two-person
row:

| SLSA asks for | This definition demands | Stage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Provenance exists, generated by the build platform | An attestation of claim `:provenance`, signed by the `ci` role, within a day of the build | `attested` |
| Provenance is authenticated and distributed | The attestation is a signed event in the ticket's own log, and it travels in the evidence bundle | `attested` |
| The build is described by its inputs | `commit` signed by `ci`, plus `artifact.digest` and a `checksums/` artifact | `built` |
| Dependencies are known | An attestation of claim `:sbom`, within a day | `attested` |
| Two-person review of what ships | `approval` signed by `release-manager`, and `[:different-person [:commit] [:approval]]` | `approved` |

A build's SLSA level is a property of the build **platform**, and no ticket
system can confer one. What this gives you instead is the thing an auditor
actually asks for months later: which rules judged this release, what evidence
was supplied, who signed it, and how to recompute the answer without trusting
anybody's word.

## Carrying the publication signature into your bundles

Adopting a definition preserves its *identity* — the address is over the parsed definition, so the pretty-printed
copy in your store hashes to the same value. It does not bring the signature,
so a bundle you produce carries the rules but not our word for them.

To carry that too, copy the signed archive alongside:

```text
cp processes/by-hash/<hash>.edn      <your-store>/processes/by-hash/
cp processes/by-hash/<hash>.sig.*    <your-store>/processes/by-hash/
cat actors >> <your-store>/actors     # so the signature has a key to check against
```

tik leaves an archive that already exists alone, and `tik bundle` ships every
file whose name starts with the pinned hash. So your evidence bundles then
carry **our signature over the rules that judged your release**, and the
recipient's `verify.sh` checks it with `ssh-keygen` and nothing else:

```text
ok    sha256-c1cffcb2….sig.e8290a63236755f2 verifies as seb
bundle: PASS
```


---

# Integrations

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/integrations/


A tik store is meant to be read by tools as readily as by people. Every
lens takes `--edn` or `--format json`, `tik serve` publishes
`/tickets.edn` and `/explain/<id>.edn`, and the frontier doubles as an
agent's authorization boundary.

- [Claude Code skill](/integrations/claude-code/) — install the plugin and
  Claude drives a store correctly, recording evidence rather than setting
  statuses.
- [Local service](/integrations/local-service/) — the board, MCP, the
  bridges, backend and notify from the native binary, under systemd.
- [MCP server](/integrations/mcp-server/) — the frontier as a gated tool
  surface over stdio.
- [Clojure library](/integrations/library/) — read, verify and derive one
  ticket in process from a JVM, babashka or native program, read-only.
- [GitHub Actions](/integrations/github-actions/) — failed workflow runs as
  tickets, one per failure streak, with `tik stats` for per-repository
  metrics.
- [GitLab pipelines](/integrations/gitlab-pipelines/) — failed pipelines as
  the same tickets, through an SSH port forward when the API only listens
  on its own host.
- [Redmine](/integrations/redmine/) — Redmine issues mirrored as tickets,
  with their history, so local work and remote tickets sit in one store.
- [Odoo](/integrations/odoo/) — Odoo project tasks mirrored as tickets,
  with their history from the chatter.


---

# Claude Code skill

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/integrations/claude-code/


Install the tik skill into [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
and Claude gains working knowledge of tik: it recognises a store, records
facts with `tik set` rather than inventing a status field, reads
`tik explain` before asking a person anything, and authors process
definitions whose stages derive from evidence instead of listing
activities.

That last part is the reason the skill exists. The failure mode for any
model writing a tik process is a task list wearing a process costume —
stages named after activities, with nothing following from anything. The
skill carries the design law that rules it out, along with the closed
guard vocabulary and the authoring loop that checks the result.

The skill lives in this repository under `skills/tik/`, packaged as a
Claude Code plugin by the manifests in `.claude-plugin/`.

## Install

Add this repository as a plugin marketplace, then install the plugin:

```text
/plugin marketplace add metio/tik
/plugin install tik@tik
```

Claude activates the skill whenever a repository holds a `tickets/` or
`.tik/` directory, an `actors` registry, or `processes/*.edn` — or when
you mention tik, tickets, processes, or stages.

## From the MCP server

A tik MCP server also serves the skill, through the MCP Skills extension
(`io.modelcontextprotocol/skills`). With the server registered, Claude
Code v2.1.331 or later lists the skill as `<server>:tik`, for example
`tik:tik`, and loads the copy built into that server, so it matches the
server's version without a plugin install. Claude Code lists MCP skills
only over MCP revision 2026-07-28, which `tik mcp` and `tik serve` speak.
See [MCP server](/integrations/mcp-server/#agent-skill) for how the
manifest is signed and checked.

## What it grants Claude

The skill teaches the CLI surface and the model behind it:

- **The daily loop** — `tik ls`, `tik next`, `tik new`, `tik set`,
  `tik explain`, `tik status`, and the selector grammar for filtering a
  board.
- **Corrections** — retract, dispute, and the fact that a dispute is
  answered only by a *different* value, so Claude does not try to clear
  one by retyping the same fact.
- **Authoring** — `tik author`, the guard vocabulary, and the lint,
  simulate, and test loop that proves a definition before a real ticket
  depends on it.
- **The one design law** — a stage is defined by what must be TRUE to
  reach it, never by who moved what.

It also knows when *not* to act: an unreachable step in `explain` means
waiting is pointless and the definition or the role register needs
fixing, not patience.

## Hearing about changes

`tik notify` runs a local notifier that re-derives and verifies every
ticket whose log changed and pushes a hint of each stage change to the
sessions that asked for it, over a Unix socket only your user can reach:

```sh
tik notify --config ~/.config/tik/notify.edn
```

```clojure
{:stores {"metio" "~/git/github.com/metio/.tik"}
 :window "PT5S"
 :sinks [{:store "metio" :where "stage=:asked"
          :command ["notify-send" "tik" "{line}"]}]}
```

A Claude Code session subscribes by running `tik notify watch` under the
Monitor tool, which feeds each output line back to Claude:

```sh
tik notify watch --store metio --where "fact:request.from=infra.run"
```

Each line is one JSON hint naming the store, the ticket, its title, the
stages it left and entered, and the actor of the event that moved it. A
hint holds no fact values and is never evidence: Claude re-derives with
`tik status` before acting on it. `tik notify channel` delivers the same
hints as a Claude Code channel to a session started with
`--dangerously-load-development-channels server:<name>`. The channel
speaks only the legacy `initialize` handshake and answers `server/discover`
with -32601. It reads at most 1 MiB per stdin line, like `tik mcp`: a
longer line, or one that is not valid JSON, answers a parse error (-32700)
whose `data.rule` names the rule, and the next line is read. Hints sent while
nobody was subscribed are not replayed, so keep a slow fallback poll. The
decisions behind this are in [ADR 0040](/decisions/0040-a-notifier-pushes-hints-not-evidence/).

## For agents generally

The skill is one surface over a derivation every tool can read. The gated
agent commands enforce the same boundary without any prompt-side
cooperation:

```sh
tik agent actions 3184 --actor bot
tik agent set 3184 severity=:high --actor bot
```

An agent sees only what the frontier admits for its role, and anything
else is refused with the derived reason. Because the boundary is the
derivation rather than an instruction, it cannot be talked around.

This site also publishes `/llms.txt` and `/llms-full.txt`, so a model can
read the documentation directly.


---

# Clojure library

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/integrations/library/


`tik.api` gives a JVM, babashka or native-image program the answers of
`tik status` and `tik verify` for one ticket without running the CLI. It
never writes to the store, signs, runs a probe, touches the network or
starts a process.

```clojure
(require '[tik.api :as api])

(def store (api/open-store "/path/to/.tik"))   ; the dir holding tickets/ or tik.db

(api/derive store "f106aa78")
;; => {:ticket #uuid "f106aa78-…" :title "…"
;;     :rules {:process :skilled-change :version 2 :hash "sha256-…"}
;;     :current [:scoped] :reached [:scoped]
;;     :facts {[:kind] {:status :present :value :feat :by "claude"} …}
;;     :missing-parents nil
;;     :definition {:pinned "sha256-…" :derived-under "sha256-…" :source :archive}
;;     :at #inst "…"}

(:ok? (api/verify-ticket store "f106aa78"))
```

Add tik as a git dependency in `deps.edn`:

```clojure
{:deps {io.github.metio/tik {:git/sha "<commit>"}}}
```

## The calls

- `(open-store root)` or `(open-store root {:limits {…}})` opens the store
  whose root is `root`, the directory holding `tickets/` (file store) or
  `tik.db` (SQLite store). Nothing is discovered from parent directories.
- `(resolve-id store ref)` takes a uuid, the full id, or a prefix of at
  least 8 characters naming exactly one ticket.
- `(ticket store ref)` returns the ticket's events in reduction order.
- `(derive store ref {:at instant})` returns the ticket's title, rules,
  current and reached stages and facts. They equal what
  `tik status <id> --edn --at <instant>` prints. When the definition found
  in the store does not hash to the ticket's pin, `derive` refuses unless
  `{:allow-unpinned-definition true}` is passed.
- `(verify-ticket store ref)` runs the `tik verify` ladder for that ticket
  with the same code as the CLI and returns it as data: `:ok?`,
  `:failures`, one summary per event (`:integrity` and `:signature`, which
  is `:verified`, `:delegated`, `:unsigned`, `:unchecked` or `:failed`)
  and every check as an item.

`tik.api/version` is the contract's version; it changes only when a
documented key, argument or refusal changes meaning or goes away.

## Refusals

Every refusal is an `ex-info` whose `:type` is in the `tik.api` namespace:
`not-a-store`, `ambiguous-store`, `backend-unavailable`,
`invalid-argument`, `invalid-id`, `unknown-ticket`, `ambiguous-id` (with
`:candidates`), `too-large` (with `:limit` and `:actual`), `unreadable`,
`definition-missing`, `definition-mismatch`, `malformed-roles`,
`underivable` and `read-only`.

## Differences from the CLI

- Signatures are verified in process (Ed25519, Ed25519 security keys,
  ML-DSA-65). A key type only ssh-keygen reads is `:unchecked`, and its
  check fails where `tik verify` would ask ssh-keygen.
- Every event, sidecar and config file is measured before it is read, and
  a symbolic link inside a ticket directory is refused. The defaults are
  `tik.api/default-limits`.
- A SQLite store is opened read-only and needs the SQLite driver, which
  babashka lacks. A native image that reads SQLite stores or identity
  bindings must require `tik.store.sqlite-jdbc` or `cheshire.core` at
  build time.

The reasoning is recorded in
[ADR 0044](/decisions/0044-a-library-reads-one-ticket-and-never-writes/).


---

# GitHub Actions

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/integrations/github-actions/


```sh
tik bridge github --config github.edn             # poll once
tik bridge github --config github.edn --webhook   # serve workflow_run deliveries
```

`tik bridge github` turns failed GitHub Actions runs into tickets under the
`ci-failure` process. One ticket covers one failure streak: the consecutive
failed runs of one workflow on one branch, from the first failure after a
green run up to the next green run. Further failures attach to the open
ticket as `ci/run/<id>/<attempt>` artifacts, the next green run is
recorded as `forge.green-run`, and a failure after that opens a new ticket.
Cancelled, skipped and neutral runs neither extend nor end a streak.
[GitLab pipelines](/integrations/gitlab-pipelines/) feed the same process
with the same facts, so the metrics below cover both forges.

## Configuration

```clojure
{:repos   ["metio/tik" {:repo "metio/jaas" :branches ["main" "next"]}]
 :orgs    ["metio" "sebhoss"]       ; every non-archived repository, default branch
 :exclude ["metio/scratch"]
 :token   {:env "GITHUB_TOKEN"}     ; or {:command …} / {:file …} / {:credential …}
 :tokens  {"sebhoss" {:command ["pass" "show" "github/sebhoss"]}}
 :api     "https://api.github.com"  ; a GitHub Enterprise Server URL also works
 :actor   "github"
 :actions {:process   :ci-failure
           :lookback  "P14D"        ; streaks with no run newer than this are left alone
           :max-pages 5             ; history pages fetched to find a streak's first run
           :failing   #{"failure" "timed_out" "startup_failure"}
           :green     #{"success"}}
 :webhook {:secret {:env "GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET"} :port 8787}}
```

Each source is enabled by its block; `:actions` is the only source so far.
A token needs read access to Actions and metadata on the repositories it
covers. `:tokens` maps a repository owner to its own token, because a
fine-grained GitHub token is scoped to one resource owner; owners without
an entry use `:token`, then `$GITHUB_TOKEN`. An `:orgs` entry may also name
a user account: its public repositories are listed, plus its private ones
when that owner's token belongs to the user. A failure listing one owner is
reported and skips that owner only.

The bridge actor (`github` by default) must be registered in `actors` with
the key in `TIK_KEY`. The `ci-failure` process's `:bridge` role holds only
the forge bridges (`github`, `gitlab`), so nobody else can open or recover
a streak.

Each ticket records `forge.host`, `forge.repo`, `forge.owner`,
`forge.workflow`, `forge.branch`, `forge.first-run` and `forge.head-sha`,
plus `repo`, the repository's name as a keyword (`:tik`): the value `tik
new` records for a ticket made inside the checkout. A store above many
checkouts therefore shows a repository's CI failures next to its other
tickets (`tik ls --all --where 'fact:repo=:tik'`).

## Polling and webhooks

Both drivers run the same sync and are idempotent, so they can run side by
side and on several replicas. A ticket id hashes the repository id,
workflow, branch and first failed run. A ticket is dated by the creation
time of its first failed run, and each later event by the start time of
the run attempt it records. GitHub never changes either timestamp, whereas
it does rewrite `updated_at` on old runs. Two replicas syncing the same
history therefore write identical events, and a re-poll writes nothing.
Time to `:recovered` runs from the first failed run's creation to the
start of the green run.

Run both from `tik backend` (`pipelines.edn`):

```clojure
{:pipelines
 [{:id :github-poll    :every "PT10M" :run ["bridge" "github"] :as "github"}
  {:id :github-webhook :watch true    :run ["bridge" "github" "--webhook"] :as "github"}]}
```

For the webhook, point a repository or organization webhook at the
listener with content type `application/json`, the shared secret, and the
*Workflow runs* event. Deliveries without a valid `X-Hub-Signature-256` are
refused with 401. A delivery only names the workflow; the bridge then reads
that workflow's history from the API, so a lost delivery is repaired by the
next poll.

A streak whose first run lies beyond `:max-pages` of history is skipped
with a message instead of being opened on a guessed start, because a
guessed start would give replicas different ticket ids.

## Triage

The cause is the one fact the forge cannot supply:

```sh
tik set <id> cause=dependency   # flaky | code | dependency | config | infra | upstream
```

A ticket reaches `:resolved` once it has both a cause and a bridge-signed
green run.

## Metrics

`tik stats` groups any tickets by a fact and derives the counts and the time
from creation to a stage:

```sh
tik stats --by forge.repo --split cause --until :resolved --where 'fact:forge.workflow'
tik stats --by forge.host --until :recovered
tik stats --by forge.repo --format json
```

The columns are the ticket count, how many have not reached the stage, and
the median, 90th-percentile and mean time to reach it. The
`fact:forge.workflow` term restricts the count to CI-failure tickets. Every number is recomputed
from the ticket logs on each run.


---

# GitLab pipelines

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/integrations/gitlab-pipelines/


```sh
tik bridge gitlab --config gitlab.edn   # poll once
```

`tik bridge gitlab` turns failed GitLab pipelines into `ci-failure`
tickets, with the same streak rules, facts and metrics as
[GitHub Actions](/integrations/github-actions/). A pipeline has no
workflow id; its source (`push`, `schedule`, `web`, …) takes that place,
so a failing nightly schedule and green push pipelines on the same branch
are separate streaks, titled `push pipeline`, `schedule pipeline` and so
on. Pipelines with any status other than `failed` and `success` (canceled,
skipped, manual) neither extend nor end a streak.

## Configuration

```clojure
{:url        "https://gitlab.example"   ; the web URL; the API is <url>/api/v4
 :membership true                       ; every project the token's account is a member of
 :groups     ["team/platform"]          ; every project of a group and its subgroups
 :projects   ["team/app" {:project "team/lib" :branches ["main" "next"]}]
 :exclude    ["team/platform/scratch"]
 :token      {:env "GITLAB_TOKEN"}      ; or {:command …} / {:file …} / {:credential …}
 :tunnel     {:ssh "admin@gitlab.example" :target "127.0.0.1:8080"}
 :actor      "gitlab"
 :pipelines  {:process   :ci-failure
              :lookback  "P14D"
              :max-pages 5
              :failing   #{"failed"}
              :green     #{"success"}}}
```

The token needs read access to the API (`read_api`). Archived projects
are left out, and a project without `:branches` watches its default branch.
A failure listing one group or project is reported and skips it only.

## SSH port forward

Some GitLab instances only serve their API on the host itself. With
`:tunnel`, the bridge runs `ssh -N -L 127.0.0.1:<free port>:<target>
<ssh>` for the duration of the sweep and sends the API requests to the
local end. The forwarded target speaks plain HTTP; the connection that
leaves the machine is the SSH one. Outside a tunnel, the bridge refuses a
non-HTTPS API URL. The SSH destination must be an account allowed to
forward ports, and ssh runs with `BatchMode=yes`, so its key must be
usable without a prompt (an agent or an unencrypted key).

## Retried pipelines

A retried pipeline keeps its id and shows only its latest outcome, so the
bridge checks every green pipeline for a ticket opened on it and records
the recovery there. GitLab's pipeline list carries no start time, so such
a recovery is dated by the pipeline's creation and its time to
`:recovered` reads as zero.


---

# Local service

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/integrations/local-service/


The native binary runs everything a long-running local install needs:
`tik serve` for the board and MCP, `tik bridge <kind>` sweeps, `tik
backend` for scheduled pipelines and `tik notify` for hints. It needs no
JVM, no babashka and no checkout. Every release checks this with
`dev/native-smoke.sh`, which drives the built binary through each of
these against loopback stand-ins for GitHub, GitLab, Redmine, Odoo and an
IMAP mailbox.

## The environment

| Variable | Read by | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `TIK_ROOT` | every verb | The store. Without it, tik uses the nearest ancestor holding `.tik/`, `tickets/` or `tik.db`. |
| `TIK_ACTOR` | every write | The actor events are signed as. `--actor` overrides it. |
| `TIK_KEY` | every write | The ed25519 private key that signs. `--key` overrides it. |
| `GITHUB_TOKEN` | `bridge github` | The token when `github.edn` names neither `:token` nor `:tokens`. |
| `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | `bridge github --webhook` | The HMAC secret when `github.edn` has no `:webhook {:secret …}`. |
| `GITLAB_TOKEN` | `bridge gitlab` | The token when `gitlab.edn` has no `:token`. |
| `REDMINE_API_KEY` | `bridge redmine` | The key when `redmine.edn` has no `:key`. |
| `ODOO_PASSWORD` | `bridge odoo` | The password when `odoo.edn` has no `:password`. |
| `CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY` | any `{:credential …}` | Set by systemd for `LoadCredential=`. |
| `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, `XDG_STATE_HOME` | `notify` | The default socket directory and the cursor. |

Any secret in a bridge config can be a spec instead of a literal:
`{:command "pass show github"}` (the first line of the command's
output), `{:file "/run/secrets/x"}`, `{:env "NAME"}` or `{:credential
"NAME"}`. The credential form is the one to prefer under systemd: the
secret never sits in a file you commit, in the environment or in argv.
An unset variable, a missing file, a failing command and an empty or
blank value are refused rather than read as an empty secret. A command
has one minute to answer, its error output goes to tik's stderr instead
of into the refusal, and a file, credential or output longer than 64 KiB
is refused.

## The board and MCP

```sh
openssl rand -hex 32 > ~/.local/state/tik/mcp-token
TIK_ROOT=~/work/.tik TIK_ACTOR=claude TIK_KEY=~/.config/tik/claude_ed25519 \
  tik serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 7777 \
    --mcp-token-file ~/.local/state/tik/mcp-token --surfaces http,mcp
```

`/` is the board, `/tickets.edn` and `/explain/<id>.edn` its data, and
`/mcp` the MCP endpoint. Clients send the token as `Authorization: Bearer
<token>`. `/mcp` answers both the `initialize` handshake and stateless
2026-07-28 requests; see [MCP server](/integrations/mcp-server/). Calls
on `/mcp` write as `TIK_ACTOR`, which is why the token is required and why
`serve` listens on 127.0.0.1 unless `--host` says otherwise.

## The bridges

Each sync bridge reads its config from the store root (`github.edn`,
`gitlab.edn`, `redmine.edn`, `odoo.edn`, `imap.edn`), or from `--config`,
sweeps once and exits 0, or 1 when any unit of the sweep failed:

```sh
export TIK_ROOT=~/work/.tik TIK_KEY=~/.config/tik/github_ed25519
tik bridge github                       # github.edn: :token or GITHUB_TOKEN
tik bridge gitlab                       # gitlab.edn: :token or GITLAB_TOKEN
tik bridge redmine                      # redmine.edn: :key or REDMINE_API_KEY
tik bridge odoo                         # odoo.edn: :password or ODOO_PASSWORD
tik bridge imap                         # imap.edn: {:imap {:host … :user … :password …}}
```

The actor of a sweep is the config's `:actor` (or `github`, `gitlab`,
`redmine`, `odoo`), so `TIK_KEY` must be that actor's key. A server that
cannot be reached, or whose certificate does not chain to a CA the binary
trusts, fails the sweep with a line naming the API, the address and the
cause, and nothing is written. For a server behind a private CA, name a
trust store holding that CA; the binary reads `-D` system properties
before its verb:

```sh
tik -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=/etc/pki/internal.p12 \
    -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=changeit bridge odoo
```

The detail of each bridge is on its own page:
[GitHub Actions](/integrations/github-actions/),
[GitLab pipelines](/integrations/gitlab-pipelines/),
[Redmine](/integrations/redmine/) and [Odoo](/integrations/odoo/).

## Under systemd

A timer per bridge, with the signing key and the remote's secret handed
over as credentials. The key file is readable only by the unit while it
runs:

```ini
# ~/.config/systemd/user/tik-bridge@.service
[Unit]
Description=Sweep the %i tik bridge
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
EnvironmentFile=%h/.config/tik/bridge-%i.env
LoadCredential=tik-key:%h/.config/tik/%i_ed25519
Environment=TIK_KEY=%d/tik-key
ExecStart=%h/.local/bin/tik bridge ${TIK_BRIDGE}
```

```ini
# ~/.config/systemd/user/tik-bridge@.timer
[Unit]
Description=Sweep the %i tik bridge every 10 minutes

[Timer]
OnBootSec=2min
OnUnitActiveSec=10min

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
```

```sh
# ~/.config/tik/bridge-github-work.env
TIK_BRIDGE=github
TIK_ROOT=/home/me/work/.tik
```

`%d` is the unit's credentials directory. A secret the config fetches
with `{:credential "github-token"}` arrives the same way, through another
`LoadCredential=github-token:<file>` line. Enable one instance per bridge
with `systemctl --user enable --now tik-bridge@github-work.timer`.

The board runs as a plain service:

```ini
# ~/.config/systemd/user/tik.service
[Unit]
Description=tik board and MCP on 127.0.0.1:7777

[Service]
Environment=TIK_ROOT=%h/work/.tik TIK_ACTOR=claude
LoadCredential=tik-key:%h/.config/tik/claude_ed25519
LoadCredential=mcp-token:%h/.local/state/tik/mcp-token
Environment=TIK_KEY=%d/tik-key
ExecStart=%h/.local/bin/tik serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 7777 \
  --mcp-token-file %d/mcp-token --surfaces http,mcp
# tik exits with 143 on the SIGTERM of a stop, which is no failure.
SuccessExitStatus=143
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target
```

## Pipelines instead of timers

`tik backend` runs the same sweeps from one process on an interval. Each
pipeline runs as the actor its `:as` names, passed as `--actor`, which
takes precedence over a bridge config's `:actor`. `TIK_KEY` is that
actor's key, so one backend process signs as one actor, and the bridge
role of each process (`roles.edn`) has to include it. Put
`pipelines.edn` at the store root:

```clojure
{:pipelines
 [{:id :github  :every "PT10M" :as "tik-backend" :run ["bridge" "github"]}
  {:id :redmine :every "PT10M" :as "tik-backend" :run ["bridge" "redmine"]}
  {:id :board   :watch true                      :run ["serve" "--port" "7777"]}]}
```

```sh
TIK_ROOT=~/work/.tik TIK_KEY=~/.config/tik/backend_ed25519 tik backend
```

A failing pipeline logs and the others carry on; a `:watch` pipeline is
restarted with backoff when it exits.

## Several stores in one backend

A config with `:stores` serves several stores from one process. Each
store signs with its own key as its own actor, and its board and MCP
answer below `/s/<store>/` with that store's own token:

```clojure
;; ~/.config/tik/backend.edn
{:stores {:work {:root "~/work/.tik" :org "work" :actor "claude"
                 :key {:credential "tik-work-key"}
                 :mcp-token-file "~/.local/state/tik/mcp-token-work"}
          :home {:root "~/home/.tik" :org "home" :actor "claude"
                 :key {:command ["pass" "show" "tik/home"]}}}
 :serve {:host "127.0.0.1" :port 7777}
 :notify {}
 :pipelines [{:id :github-work :store :work :every "PT10M" :run ["bridge" "github"]}]}
```

```sh
tik backend --config ~/.config/tik/backend.edn
```

- `:key` is a path, `{:file …}`, `{:credential …}` or `{:command …}`.
  A command's whole output is written to an owner-only file below
  `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` for as long as the backend runs. `{:env …}` is
  refused.
- At start, each key must sign as the store's `:actor` according to that
  store's own `actors` file. Two stores with different `:org` may not
  resolve to the same key unless `:allow-shared-keys [[:work :home]]`
  says so.
- An MCP token file must hold at least 32 characters and be readable by
  you only, and each store needs its own. A token sent to another store's
  path is refused with 401.
- A pipeline names its `:store`. It runs as that store's actor, or as
  `:as`, which that store's `actors` file must grant the key to. It may
  not pass `--key`, `--actor` or `--config`, and may not run `serve`,
  `notify`, `mcp` or `backend`, which the backend provides for every
  store itself.
- `:notify` takes the settings of a `notify.edn` and watches every store
  of the backend.
- `TIK_ROOT`, `TIK_KEY`, `TIK_PQ_KEY` and `TIK_ACTOR` must not be set in
  the backend's environment, and neither may `GITHUB_TOKEN`,
  `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, `GITLAB_TOKEN`, `REDMINE_API_KEY` or
  `ODOO_PASSWORD`: every pipeline inherits the environment, so a token
  meant for one store's bridge would reach all of them. Name the secret
  in the bridge's config instead.

Any problem with any store refuses the whole backend and lists every
problem, so a running backend always serves every store it names.

## Bridges and mailboxes as pipelines

A multi-store backend replaces one systemd timer per bridge. Each run of
a pipeline is a child process of the same binary that sees only its own
store's root, key and actor, so a bridge signs as its own delegate in its
own store, and nothing one run keeps in memory reaches another store's.

```clojure
{:stores {...}
 :on-failure {:run ["notify-send" "--urgency=critical" "tik {store}/{pipeline}" "{reason}"]
              :repeat "PT1H"}
 :pipelines
 [{:id :github-work :store :work :every "PT10M" :as "github"
   :key {:credential "github-work-key"} :config "github.edn" :run ["bridge" "github"]}
  {:id :redmine-work :store :work :every "PT10M" :jitter "PT2M" :timeout "PT5M" :as "redmine"
   :key {:credential "redmine-work-key"} :run ["bridge" "redmine"]}
  {:id :support-mail :store :work :watch true :as "mail"
   :key {:credential "mail-work-key"} :config "imap.edn" :run ["bridge" "imap" "--watch"]}]}
```

| Key | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `:every` | The interval of a scheduled pipeline, as an ISO-8601 duration. Fires sit on a grid from the backend's start, so they do not drift by the run time. | |
| `:jitter` | Each fire lands at a random point within this window after its grid point. | `PT1M`, at most half of `:every` |
| `:timeout` | A run still going after this is stopped (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL five seconds later) and counts as failed. | `:every` |
| `:watch` | A continuous pipeline, restarted after 1 s, doubling to 60 s while it keeps failing fast, and back to 1 s once a run lasted a minute. | |
| `:config` | The verb's config file, relative to the store's root, absolute, or `~/…`; it must exist when the backend starts. | the verb's default file at the store's root |
| `:as`, `:key` | The delegate the run signs as, and its key, which the store's `actors` file must grant to it. | the store's actor and key |

The backend's own keys:

- **No overlap.** A pipeline due while its previous run still goes is not
  started again; the skip is logged and the next fire is its next grid
  point. Different pipelines run at the same time.
- **Catch-up.** Fires missed while the backend was stopped or the machine
  slept collapse into one run, which lands within the jitter window of the
  moment the backend noticed, at most 30 seconds after a resume.
- **`:on-failure`** runs a command, without a shell, when a run fails or
  times out, with `{store}`, `{pipeline}`, `{exit}` and `{reason}` filled
  in. A pipeline is reported when it starts failing and again every
  `:repeat` while it keeps failing; `"PT0S"` reports every failure, as a
  unit's `OnFailure=` does.
- **The journal.** Every line is labelled `[store/pipeline]`, and under
  systemd it carries a priority, so `journalctl --user -u tik-backend -p
  warning` shows the pipelines' error output and the failure reports.
- **`:exec`** names the command that runs this tik. The native binary and
  babashka find themselves; set it when neither applies.

Two pipelines of stores with different `:org` may not sign with the same
key unless `:allow-shared-keys` names the pair of stores: one
organisation's delegate never signs for another's.

### Mailboxes

`bridge imap` reads one mailbox under `:imap`, or several under
`:mailboxes`. Every other top-level key is a default for each mailbox, so
adding a support address is one more list entry:

```clojure
;; imap.edn at the store's root
{:dkim {:require true :authserv-id "mx.example.org"}
 :default-actor "mail"
 :mailboxes
 [{:id "support-example-org" :process :support
   :imap {:host "imap.example.org" :user "support@example.org"
          :password {:command ["pass" "show" "mail/support@example.org"]}}}
  {:id "support-app" :process :app-support
   :imap {:host "imap.example.org" :user "support@app.example"
          :password {:credential "support-app-imap"}}}]}
```

Each mailbox has its own connection, its own backoff and its own
`:process`, and its lines are labelled with its `:id`. `bridge imap
--mailbox <id>` reads only that one. A `:mailboxes` list, and every
mailbox a backend watches, must:

- require DKIM at a pinned verifier, `:dkim {:require true :authserv-id
  …}`, the id your receiving MX stamps on `Authentication-Results`, so a
  forged From is never credited to anybody (see below);
- take its password from `{:command …}`, `{:credential …}` or `{:file
  …}`, never a literal and never `{:env …}`;
- under a backend, be signed by a key the store grants to every actor a
  mailbox records mail as: `:default-actor` and each `:from->actor` value.

#### The DKIM verdict

tik reads only the topmost `Authentication-Results` header of a message,
the first one in its header block. The MTA that delivered the message
prepended that header above every header the sender wrote, so a sender
cannot place a header above it. When the topmost header names a verifier
other than `:authserv-id`, the message is refused, even if a header
further down claims the trusted id and `dkim=pass`. The From domain must
then be the `header.d` of a `dkim=pass` in that header, or a subdomain
of it.

This holds only when your receiving MTA stamps every message it
delivers. A message it delivers without a header of its own keeps the
sender's headers on top, and a forged header there is read as the
verdict. Check how your provider treats mail between two of its own
customers before you rely on the gate.

`:authserv-id` takes one of:

- a string, compared with the whole id, ignoring case:
  `"mx.example.org"`;
- a pattern, `{:pattern "mx[0-9]+\\.example\\.org"}`, matched against
  the whole id, ignoring case;
- a list of both: `["mx.example.org" {:pattern "…"}]`.

A pattern always matches the whole id, so `mx[0-9]+\.example\.org`
never accepts `evil.mx1.example.org` or `mx1.example.org.attacker.test`.
It may use letters, digits and `-`, `\.` for a dot, `\d`, character
classes such as `[0-9]`, groups with alternatives such as `(mx|smtp)`,
and the quantifiers `?`, `*`, `+` and `{n,m}`. It must end in a literal
domain of at least two labels, such as `\.example\.org`. An unescaped
`.`, `^`, `$`, a top-level `|`, inline flags and any other construct are
refused when the config loads, and so is a pattern that matches an empty
id.

Some providers stamp the name of the receiving MX host rather than one
id for the domain. Migadu stamps `mx13.migadu.com` or a sibling host,
whichever received the message, so pin it with a pattern:

```clojure
{:dkim {:require true :authserv-id {:pattern "mx[0-9]+\\.migadu\\.com"}}}
```

Migadu was seen adding no `Authentication-Results` header to mail sent
from one Migadu mailbox to another, so such mail is refused. If Migadu
also keeps an `Authentication-Results` header that a Migadu-hosted
sender wrote into such a mail, that forged header is the topmost one;
whether it does has not been checked.

Every IMAP and POP3 connection checks that the server's certificate is
trusted and names the host, and plaintext (`:tls false`) is refused for
any host that is not written as a loopback address (`localhost`,
`127.x.x.x`, `::1`).

### Under systemd

One unit replaces the board's service and every bridge timer. The keys
of the delegates arrive as credentials; the store keys come from a
password manager here, and `{:credential …}` works for them as well:

```ini
# ~/.config/systemd/user/tik-backend.service
[Unit]
Description=tik: the boards, MCP, bridges, mailboxes and notifier of every local store
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=%h/.local/bin/tik backend --config %h/.config/tik/backend.edn
LoadCredential=github-work-key:%h/.config/tik/github-work_ed25519
LoadCredential=redmine-work-key:%h/.config/tik/redmine-work_ed25519
LoadCredential=mail-work-key:%h/.config/tik/mail-work_ed25519
LoadCredential=support-app-imap:%h/.config/tik/support-app-imap
# the MCP tokens live here; the backend refuses a token others can read
StateDirectory=tik-backend
StateDirectoryMode=0700
# tik exits with 143 on the SIGTERM of a stop, which is no failure.
SuccessExitStatus=143
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=10
# a stop also ends every run the backend started
KillMode=control-group

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target
```

The backend refuses `TIK_ROOT` and the bridges' token variables, so the
unit sets none of them. Disable the bridge timers and the old board
service when it starts, and point MCP clients at `/s/<store>/mcp`.

### Reporter pseudonyms and block lists

A mailbox can record who sent each report without writing the address
into the store, and refuse senders who only send garbage. Both keys go
on a mailbox or at the top level as a default for all of them:

```clojure
{:reporter {:key {:credential "reporter-key"}
            :table "~/.local/state/tik/reporters"
            :fact [:reporter :id]}
 :block {:addresses ["noise@example.net"]
         :domains ["spam.example"]
         :pseudonyms ["hmac-sha256:<64 hex digits>"]}}
```

With `:reporter`, a new ticket from a sender the DKIM gate authenticated
carries the fact `[:reporter :id]` (or the `:fact` you name) holding
`hmac-sha256:` and the hex HMAC-SHA256 of the lower-cased address under
your key. Without the key nobody can reverse it; with it, a guessed
address can be checked, so guard the key like a signing key. It comes
from `{:command …}`, `{:credential …}` or `{:file …}`, holds at least 32
bytes (`openssl rand -hex 32` prints 64), and is resolved once when the
bridge starts. The bridge refuses to start when `:reporter` lacks a key,
lacks `:dkim {:require true …}`, puts its table inside the store, or
names a process that does not declare the fact with a schema a
pseudonym satisfies:

```clojure
:process/facts {[:reporter :id] [:re "^hmac-sha256:[0-9a-f]{64}$"]}
```

A comment on an existing ticket records no pseudonym, and a `tik>` line
in a mail can never set the reporter fact.

The table maps each pseudonym to its address and the time it was first
seen. It is a directory only you can enter (0700), one file per
pseudonym (0600), and it stays on this machine, outside the store, so it
is never committed or pushed:

- `tik reporter show <pseudonym>` resolves one;
- `tik reporter forget <address|pseudonym>` deletes its rows for an
  erasure request, after which the pseudonym on the tickets resolves to
  nothing (backups of the table keep what they hold until they expire);
- `tik reporter stats [--format json]` counts tickets per pseudonym,
  showing the address where a row exists and `(forgotten)` where none
  does.

Each takes `--table <dir>`, or reads the table from `--config <imap.edn>`
(by default `imap.edn`, else `bridge.edn`, at the store's root) with
`--mailbox <id>` when the config names several.

`:block` refuses a sender after the DKIM gate and before anything is
written; the poll logs the rule that matched, never the address or the
body, and goes on with the next message. A domain matches itself and
every subdomain on a label boundary, so `spam.example` also blocks
`mail.spam.example` and not `nospam.example`. Listing `:pseudonyms`
keeps plaintext out of the config and needs `:reporter`, whose key
computes a sender's pseudonym; a block by pseudonym still holds after
the sender's row was forgotten.

## Hints

```sh
tik notify --config ~/.config/tik/notify.edn          # the notifier
tik notify watch --store work --where "stage=:asked"  # one JSON line per hint
```

See [Claude Code](/integrations/claude-code/) for the notifier's config
and what a hint holds.


---

# MCP server

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/integrations/mcp-server/


```sh
TIK_ACTOR=bot TIK_KEY=~/.config/tik/bot_ed25519 tik mcp
```

`tik mcp` speaks the Model Context Protocol over stdio and exposes one
store as a tool surface. The tools an agent is offered are exactly the
steps the frontier admits for its role at that moment, so the tool list
*is* the authorization boundary.

## One shared server over HTTP

```sh
TIK_ACTOR=bot TIK_KEY=~/.config/tik/bot_ed25519 \
  tik serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 7777 --mcp-token-file ~/.local/state/tik/mcp-token
```

`tik serve` also speaks MCP on `/mcp` when given a token file, so every
client shares one long-running server instead of starting its own
process. It answers one JSON-RPC message per POST with JSON and opens no
event stream. A request needs the token as `Authorization: Bearer …`, and
one whose `Origin` is not the server's own is refused, which keeps a web
page from driving the server through DNS rebinding. The token must be at
least 32 characters; `openssl rand -hex 32` makes one.

Without `--host`, a server offering MCP listens on 127.0.0.1 only, because
`/mcp` writes over plain HTTP; put a TLS proxy in front before offering it
beyond the machine. The board alone keeps listening on every address.

`--surfaces` picks what the server offers: `http` for the read-only board
and its EDN, `mcp` for the tools, or `http,mcp`. Without it, the server
offers `http`, and `mcp` too when a token file is given.

## Agent skill

The server serves tik's agent skill, the repository's `skills/tik/` tree
as built into the binary, through the MCP Skills extension
(`io.modelcontextprotocol/skills`):

- `skills/list` and `skills/get` return the skill's entry: its
  frontmatter and a manifest listing every file with its sha256 digest
  and size.
- `resources/read` serves the files under `skill://tik/<path>`. A client
  without the extension sees them as ordinary resources, and the server
  instructions name `skill://tik/SKILL.md`.
- A URI with a `..` or `.` segment, an empty segment or an escaped
  character is refused, as is a skill name other than lowercase letters,
  digits and single inner hyphens, and any file the manifest does not
  list.

The extension's digests only show that a file matches the manifest, and
whoever runs the server writes both. tik therefore signs the manifest
with `TIK_KEY` as `TIK_ACTOR`, in the SSHSIG namespace
`tik-skill-manifest`, and puts the signature in the entry's `_meta` under
`wtf.metio/skill-manifest`. Without a key, that marker says
`"signed": false` and why. `tik skill verify` checks a server against the
store's `actors` file:

```sh
tik skill verify http://127.0.0.1:7777/mcp --token-file ~/.local/state/tik/mcp-token
```

It checks the signature, then reads every file and compares its bytes,
and the SKILL.md frontmatter, with the manifest. It exits 1 for an
unsigned manifest, a signature no registered actor made, or any file
that differs. Given a saved `skills/list` or `skills/get` response
instead of a URL, it checks the signature alone. It accepts signatures in
the namespaces `tik-skill-manifest` and `kajero-skill-manifest`, and a
manifest that lists more than 512 files, declares a skill over 16 MiB,
names an entry URI other than the skill's `SKILL.md` or lists a file of
another skill is malformed.

The signed bytes are the manifest in a fixed form, one line each:
`skill-manifest v1`, `skill <SKILL.md URI>`, then
`file <digest> <size> <URI>` per file in URI order, each line ending in
a newline. The form leaves out the frontmatter, which a client compares
against the signed SKILL.md bytes, and binds no server version, so an
older signed manifest still verifies until its signer is removed from
`actors`.

The server speaks both MCP eras: the `initialize` handshake of revisions
up to 2025-06-18, and revision 2026-07-28, whose every request carries
its version and capabilities in `_meta`. Claude Code lists a server's
skills only over 2026-07-28. Over HTTP, a 2026-07-28 request must repeat
its version, method and resource or tool name in the
`MCP-Protocol-Version`, `Mcp-Method` and `Mcp-Name` headers, and is
refused with `400` when they differ from the body.

A message is one JSON object of at most 1 MiB, read strictly: a key named
twice, text after the value or a body over the limit answers a parse
error (`-32700`) whose `data.rule` names the rule, without quoting the
input. A request without `"jsonrpc": "2.0"`, a string method and a string
or integer `id` answers `-32600`, an unknown method `-32601`, and an
unknown tool or `arguments` that are not an object `-32602`. A tool that
runs and fails, such as a refused assertion or a missing argument,
answers in its result with `isError`. A notification, a message without
an `id`, runs nothing and gets no answer (`202` over HTTP). Over stdio, a
line over the limit is refused without being held in memory, and the
next line is read as usual.

## Why the boundary holds

An agent's permission to act is derived from the same guards a person's
is. A step whose `:signed-by` names a role the agent is not in never
appears as an available tool, and calling it anyway is refused with the
derived reason rather than a generic denial.

That matters because the alternative — telling a model in its prompt what
it may not do — is enforcement by cooperation. Here the check happens
where the answer is computed, and it produces the same reason string a
person would see.

## Accountability

Every write the agent makes is an ordinary signed event with the agent's
own actor identity. The log therefore distinguishes what a person claimed
from what an agent claimed, permanently and without a separate audit
trail. `tik causal` names the events behind each reached stage, so a
conclusion an agent contributed to can be traced to the evidence it
supplied and the key that signed it.

## Task specifications from guards

An agent asking "what should I do?" gets the same structured answer every
other lens renders:

```sh
tik explain 3184 --actor bot --edn
```

Each missing step carries its path, its schema, and who may satisfy it —
which makes an acceptance criterion out of a guard, rather than out of a
sentence somebody wrote in a ticket description.


---

# Odoo

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/integrations/odoo/


```sh
tik bridge odoo --config odoo.edn                               # poll once
tik bridge odoo describe --model project.task --config odoo.edn # read a model's fields
```

`tik bridge odoo` mirrors Odoo project tasks into the store as tickets
under the `odoo-task` process. Each ticket carries the task's title,
stage, assignee and project as facts signed by the bridge, its
conversation as artifacts, and its URL as `odoo.url`. The stage follows
the mirrored Odoo stage: `:closed` when the configuration names that stage
as closed, `:open` for every other stage. Moving the task back to an open
stage in Odoo brings the ticket back to `:open` on the next sync.

Odoo stays the place where the task is worked on. Facts you add locally
(a `link.*` to another ticket, notes for yourself) stay in tik and never
move the mirrored stages.

## Configuration

```clojure
{:profile       "project.task"             ; optional; the Odoo model to mirror
 :url           "https://odoo.example"
 :db            "odoo"                     ; the database name
 :user          "you@example.com"          ; a string or a secret spec
 :password      {:env "ODOO_PASSWORD"}     ; a secret spec
 :closed-stages ["Done" "Cancelled"]       ; stage names that count as closed
 :users         {45 "seb"}                 ; Odoo user id -> tik actor
 :domain        [["user_id" "=" 45]]       ; optional; default: tasks assigned to :user
 :actor         "odoo"
 :process       :odoo-task}
```

The bridge talks to Odoo's JSON-RPC endpoint, `/jsonrpc`. Odoo 12 has no
API keys, so it logs in with the user's password and sends it with every
call; a user with read access to the tasks is enough. Odoo often refuses to
list its databases, in which case the database name shows after logging in
through the web interface (`/web/session/get_session_info` reports it as
`db`).

Odoo 12 stages carry no closed flag. Folding a stage only hides its column,
and a folded backlog is still open work, so `:closed-stages` names the
closed stages explicitly.

Each sweep syncs every task the domain selects, plus every task the store
already mirrors, so a task that is reassigned or archived keeps its ticket
current. A task counts as mirrored when the store holds its own ticket, the
one whose id the host of `:url`, the model and `odoo.id` name; `odoo.url`
plays no part, so changing the scheme, port or path of `:url` on the same
host keeps every task, and a ticket of another host or model is never
taken for one. `:users` renders an Odoo user as a tik actor in `odoo.assignee`;
other users appear under the name Odoo shows.

## Profiles

A profile describes how one Odoo model becomes tickets: which tracked
fields become which facts, which field derives the ticket's state and from
which configuration lists, how the ticket title is formed, which chatter
messages become artifacts, the default domain and the process. `:profile`
names the profile by its model, as a string or a keyword, and defaults to
`"project.task"`. A configuration that names a model without a profile is
refused when it loads, with the list of profiles there are.

| Profile | Facts | State | Title | Configuration |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `project.task` | `odoo.title`, `odoo.stage`, `odoo.assignee`, `odoo.project` | `odoo.state`: `:closed` for a stage in `:closed-stages`, else `:open` | `#<id> <title the task was created with>` | `:closed-stages` |

Every profile also asserts `odoo.id` and `odoo.url`, whose URL names the
model. The ticket id is a name-based UUID over the Odoo host, the model and
the record id, so records of two models with the same id become two
tickets.

## Describing a model

```sh
tik bridge odoo describe --model helpdesk.ticket --config odoo.edn
tik bridge odoo describe --model project.task --edn
tik bridge odoo describe --model project.task --format json
```

`tik bridge odoo describe` asks the server how it defines one model's
fields and prints, for each field, its type, label, whether it is required
or read-only, the model a relation points at, the values of a selection,
and whether Odoo tracks it. Only tracked fields can be mirrored with their
history, so this is the list to read before writing a profile for a new
model. The output also says whether the model inherits `mail.thread`.

The command writes nothing to Odoo or to the store. It logs in and calls
`version`, `login` and `fields_get`, and refuses every other call before it
leaves tik, so a write method cannot be reached from it. It reads `:url`,
`:db`, `:user` and `:password` from the same `odoo.edn` as the bridge;
`:password` has to be a secret spec such as `{:env "ODOO_PASSWORD"}` or
`{:command "pasejo secret show …"}`, and a literal password in the file is
refused. Neither the output nor an error message carries the password.

Odoo 12 reports the tracking flag as `track_visibility`, later versions as
`tracking`; the command asks for both and names the one the server
answered with. When the server reports neither, every field's tracked flag
reads `unknown`. Whether `message_post` accepts a `message_id` argument
also reads `unknown`: `fields_get` describes fields, and Odoo offers no
read-only call that reports a method's arguments.

When the model has a profile, the output ends with how the profile fits
the server: the fields it reads that the server lacks, fields whose type
differs from the one the profile declares, actor fields that do not point
at `res.users`, mirrored fields the server does not track, and, for a
state read from a selection field, the selection values no configuration
list names, which fall to the profile's default state. A stage field such
as `stage_id` is a relation, so its stage names are records that
`fields_get` cannot list.

## History

Every event is a function of the task and its chatter. Odoo records each
change of a tracked field as a tracking value in the chatter, with the old
and new value as Odoo displays them. The ticket is dated by the task's
creation and carries the values the task was created with, recovered by
undoing each tracked change from the current values. Each message then
adds its changes at its own time, and a comment or email as an
`odoo/message/<id>` artifact. A re-sync adds only the messages that are
new, and two machines syncing the same Odoo write identical events.

Only the title, stage, assignee and project are mirrored, because those
are the fields Odoo tracks. A tracking value names its field by the label
the field had at the time, in the language of whoever made the change; the
bridge reads every field's label in every installed language and leaves
out a label two fields share.

## Open work

```sh
tik ls --all --where 'stage=:open and fact:odoo.assignee=seb'
tik stats --by odoo.project --until :closed
```


---

# Redmine

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/integrations/redmine/


```sh
tik bridge redmine --config redmine.edn   # poll once
```

`tik bridge redmine` mirrors Redmine issues into the store as tickets
under the `redmine-issue` process. Each ticket carries the issue's
status, assignee, priority, tracker, project, subject and due date as
facts signed by the bridge, its description and notes as artifacts, and
its URL as `redmine.url`. The stage follows the mirrored status: `:open`,
or `:closed` when Redmine counts the status as closed. Reopening the issue
in Redmine brings the ticket back to `:open` on the next sync.

Redmine stays the place where the issue is worked on. Facts you add
locally (a `link.*` to another ticket, notes for yourself) stay in tik and
never move the mirrored stages.

## Configuration

```clojure
{:url     "https://redmine.example"
 :key     {:env "REDMINE_API_KEY"}         ; your API key (My account → API access key)
 :query   {:assigned_to_id "me"}           ; issues.json filters; all statuses are included
 :users   {11 "seb"}                       ; Redmine user id -> tik actor
 :actor   "redmine"
 :process :redmine-issue}
```

Each sweep syncs every issue the query selects, plus every issue the store
already mirrors, so an issue that is reassigned or moved keeps its ticket
current. `:users` renders a Redmine user as a tik actor in
`redmine.assignee`; other users appear under the name Redmine shows.

## History

Every event is a function of the issue and its journal. The ticket is
dated by the issue's creation and carries the values the issue was opened
with, recovered by undoing each journal entry from the current values.
Each journal entry then adds its changes at its own time, and its note as
a `redmine/journal/<id>` artifact. A re-sync adds only the entries that
are new, and two machines syncing the same Redmine write identical events.

Statuses, priorities and trackers are rendered by name from Redmine's
current configuration. Renaming one in Redmine adds assertions under the
new name on the next sync; the latest journal entry still decides the
current value.

## Open work

```sh
tik ls --all --where 'stage=:open and fact:redmine.assignee=seb'
tik stats --by redmine.project --until :closed
```
