# Runbooks

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/


A process definition names a runbook per stage through its `:hint` field, and
`tik explain` prints that link beside the missing evidence:

```text
To reach :triaged:
  ✗ set fact [:category] ([:enum :billing :technical :account :abuse])
  (see: kb/runbooks/support-request-triaged.md)
```

So these pages are read at the moment somebody is stuck, and each answers a
single question: what has to become true here, and who can make it so. They
live in the repository's knowledge bundle under `kb/runbooks/`, so a checkout,
an agent, and this site read the same document.

Each process below is listed in stage order rather than alphabetically — a
runbook makes most sense beside the stages it sits between.

## support-request

The sample process the conformance corpus pins: a customer report from arrival
to acknowledgement.

| Stage | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| [`:received`](/runbooks/support-request-received/) | A new report exists and nothing is known yet. |
| [`:triaged`](/runbooks/support-request-triaged/) | A triager has signed off a category and a severity. |
| [`:reproducible`](/runbooks/support-request-reproducible/) | A reproduction is attached under `repro/`. |
| [`:resolved`](/runbooks/support-request-resolved/) | A resolution reference points at the fix. |
| [`:escalated`](/runbooks/support-request-escalated/) | Derives on its own: 48 hours with no category. |
| [`:closed`](/runbooks/support-request-closed/) | Sticky milestone — only the customer's acknowledgement closes it. |

## release

A version's supply chain as evidence: one ticket per release, each stage
saying what must be true of the artifacts rather than which job ran.

| Stage | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| [`:built`](/runbooks/release-built/) | Artifacts exist and CI has signed which commit produced them. |
| [`:scanned`](/runbooks/release-scanned/) | A vulnerability scan came back clean, attested within the last day. |
| [`:attested`](/runbooks/release-attested/) | An SBOM, build provenance, and a signature are on record. |
| [`:published`](/runbooks/release-published/) | Sticky — a maintainer shipped it, and not the one who built it. |
| [`:withheld`](/runbooks/release-withheld/) | A maintainer decided it does not ship, with the reason. |

## tik-dev

The process tik's own development runs in; this repository is a live store.

| Stage | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| [`:captured`](/runbooks/tik-dev-captured/) | A thought exists and the ticket preserves it. |
| [`:triaged`](/runbooks/tik-dev-triaged/) | A summary and a kind are on record. |
| [`:implemented`](/runbooks/tik-dev-implemented/) | A commit is named. |
| [`:landed`](/runbooks/tik-dev-landed/) | The full local gate came back green. |
| [`:parked`](/runbooks/tik-dev-parked/) | Deliberately not now — with the reason, which is the deliverable. |

## hypothesis

Falsifiable claims carrying a kill criterion, so a plan can be wrong on
purpose rather than by accident.

| Stage | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| [`:captured`](/runbooks/hypothesis-captured/) | A belief worth testing exists, even half-formed. |
| [`:stated`](/runbooks/hypothesis-stated/) | The claim and what would kill it are both written down. |
| [`:running`](/runbooks/hypothesis-running/) | The experiment is named: what is run, on what, measured how. |
| [`:validated`](/runbooks/hypothesis-validated/) | Evidence a stranger could check. |
| [`:killed`](/runbooks/hypothesis-killed/) | Which criterion fired, and the evidence it fired on. |

## track

Two stages, for something that needs recording rather than a workflow.

| Stage | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| [`:open`](/runbooks/track-open/) | The ticket exists; record what is true as it happens. |
| [`:done`](/runbooks/track-done/) | The thing ended — say how. |

## identity-registry

| Stage | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| [`:registry`](/runbooks/identity-registry-registry/) | Always this stage: key bindings are evidence, not workflow. |

## incident-response

From first alarm to a reviewed postmortem.

| Stage | Reached when |
| --- | --- |
| [`:declared`](/runbooks/incident-declared/) | Severity and impact are on record. |
| [`:mitigated`](/runbooks/incident-mitigated/) | A commander signed the severity and the bleeding stopped. |
| [`:postmortem-due`](/runbooks/incident-postmortem-due/) | Derives from time alone: five days with no postmortem. |
| [`:analyzed`](/runbooks/incident-analyzed/) | A root cause and a postmortem summary exist. |
| [`:reviewed`](/runbooks/incident-reviewed/) | Sticky — accepted by somebody who did not write it. |

## employee-onboarding

The checklist that runs itself, two branches rejoining at the end.

| Stage | Reached when |
| --- | --- |
| [`:hired`](/runbooks/onboarding-hired/) | A start date, a signed contract, and the file to go with it. |
| [`:equipped`](/runbooks/onboarding-equipped/) | IT signed off the equipment reference. |
| [`:accounts-live`](/runbooks/onboarding-accounts/) | IT signed off the account. |
| [`:ready`](/runbooks/onboarding-ready/) | Sticky — both branches landed and a buddy is named. |

## okf-publish

Publishing a knowledge bundle, with review signed over its content hash.

| Stage | Reached when |
| --- | --- |
| [`:drafted`](/runbooks/okf-publish-drafted/) | The bundle exists and its hash is on record. |
| [`:reviewed`](/runbooks/okf-publish-reviewed/) | A reviewer vouched for it, signing over that hash. |
| [`:approved`](/runbooks/okf-publish-approved/) | An owner authorised release over the same hash. |
| [`:published`](/runbooks/okf-publish-published/) | Public — and it un-publishes if the bundle is revised. |

## renovate-migration

Moving a repository from Dependabot to Renovate, with a probe keeping it honest.

| Stage | Reached when |
| --- | --- |
| [`:planned`](/runbooks/renovate-migration-planned/) | An approach is written down. |
| [`:configured`](/runbooks/renovate-migration-configured/) | Renovate is in, Dependabot is out, and the probe agrees. |
| [`:verified`](/runbooks/renovate-migration-verified/) | A dashboard, a first PR, and a maintainer's approval. |

## supply-chain-release

A release as evidence, with four-eyes approval.

| Stage | Reached when |
| --- | --- |
| [`:built`](/runbooks/supply-chain-release-built/) | CI signed which commit produced these bytes. |
| [`:attested`](/runbooks/supply-chain-release-attested/) | An SBOM and provenance, each attested within a day. |
| [`:scanned`](/runbooks/supply-chain-release-scanned/) | A vulnerability scan came back clean, recently. |
| [`:approved`](/runbooks/supply-chain-release-approved/) | Sticky — approved by somebody who is not the pipeline. |
| [`:withheld`](/runbooks/supply-chain-release-withheld/) | A decision not to ship, with the reason on record. |

## automated-release

The same, for a pipeline that ships with no human in the loop.

| Stage | Reached when |
| --- | --- |
| [`:built`](/runbooks/automated-release-built/) | CI signed which commit produced these bytes. |
| [`:attested`](/runbooks/automated-release-attested/) | An SBOM and provenance, each attested within a day. |
| [`:scanned`](/runbooks/automated-release-scanned/) | A vulnerability scan came back clean, recently. |

## ci-failure

A failing GitHub Actions workflow, from its first failed run to a green run
with the cause on record.

| Stage | Reached when |
| --- | --- |
| [`:failing`](/runbooks/ci-failure-failing/) | The bridge signed the streak's first failed run. |
| [`:triaged`](/runbooks/ci-failure-triaged/) | A cause is on record. |
| [`:recovered`](/runbooks/ci-failure-recovered/) | The bridge signed the first green run after the streak. |
| [`:resolved`](/runbooks/ci-failure-resolved/) | Sticky — green again, with the cause on record. |


---

# automated-release / :attested

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/automated-release-attested/


# automated-release · attested

What the artifact is made of, and how it came to be — each said by a
party the registry trusts, each recent enough to be about this build.

- Record the artifact's digest and have `ci` sign it:
  `tik set <id> artifact.digest="\"sha256:…\""`.
- Bring the SBOM and the provenance in as attestations. Where the
  pipeline already emits in-toto or SLSA documents, `tik bridge intoto
  <file>` maps their `predicateType` onto the claim these guards read, so
  nothing is invented and nothing is transcribed by hand.
- Both windows are one day, and they are measured against the moment the
  attestation was written. Produce them in the release job; an older
  document describes an older build.

tik checks that a trusted attester said these things. It never reads the
SBOM and forms no opinion about its contents, so this stage is worth
exactly what the attester is worth — choose who may sign accordingly, and
say so to whoever reads the badge.

The stage is sticky, so what it asserts is "when this version shipped, a
fresh SBOM and provenance existed", which stays true. Whether today's
advisories still agree is a question about a new scan, on a new ticket.


---

# automated-release / :built

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/automated-release-built/


# automated-release · built

The pipeline says which commit produced these bytes, and hands over the
checksums that name them.

- Record the version and the commit from the pipeline's own context:
  `tik set <id> version="\"1.4.0\"" commit="\"$GITHUB_SHA\""`.
- The `commit` fact must be signed by a member of the `ci` role. Name
  yours first with `tik roles add ci <actor>` — the definition ships with
  the role empty so adoption inherits nobody else's org chart.
- Attach the checksums under a `checksums/` prefix:
  `tik attach <id> dist/SHA256SUMS --as checksums/SHA256SUMS`. The hash
  goes on the log and the blob is stored beside it, so a reader compares
  their own download against a value the signature covers.

Give `ci` a keypair generated per run and bound to the pipeline's own
workload identity — `tik bridge workload --github` binds it to the token
the platform already issues — so nothing long-lived exists to leak and
the binding is what makes the signatures checkable afterwards.

Name the subject that may bind `ci` under `:bindings` in `oidc.edn`
(ADR 0026) — `repo:<org>/<repo>:ref:refs/heads/main` for a workflow on
the default branch. Every repository on the platform can obtain a token
from the same issuer, so without that line any of them could bind `ci`.

The stage is sticky: a published version is never rebuilt, so "this
commit produced these bytes" is a fact about a moment that stays true.


---

# automated-release / :scanned

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/automated-release-scanned/


# automated-release · scanned

A vulnerability scan ran against this build and came back clean.

- Attest the scan, naming the tool and the advisory database it read:
  `tik attest <id> :vulnerability-scan --body '{:tool "…" :db "…"}'`.
- Record the outcome as a fact `ci` signs:
  `tik set <id> scan.result=:clean` — or `:findings`.

`:findings` is a legitimate outcome and belongs on the record. Let the
scanner write what it found, let the ticket carry it, and let the release
ship anyway if that is the call — the stage stays unreached and the badge
says so, which is the whole reason this stage is worth deriving. A stage
nothing could ever fail would be decoration.

Run the scan inside the release job rather than reusing an earlier
result. The one-day window exists because a scan is a claim about the
advisory database at a moment; a result from last week is
cryptographically valid, honestly stale, and silent about everything
published since.

The stage is sticky, so it asserts that the scan was clean when this
version shipped. That does not claim the version is clean today, and a
release that has aged is worth re-scanning on a ticket of its own.


---

# ci-failure / :failing

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/ci-failure-failing/


# ci-failure: failing

A CI workflow (a GitHub Actions workflow, or a GitLab pipeline source)
has been failing on this branch since the run in `forge.first-run`. The
forge bridge (`tik bridge github` or `tik bridge gitlab`) opened the ticket
and attaches every further failed run of the streak under `ci/run/`.

- Open the first run, find out why it failed, and fix it or hand it on.
- Record the cause as soon as it is known (see `:triaged`).


---

# ci-failure / :recovered

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/ci-failure-recovered/


# ci-failure: recovered

The workflow passed again on this branch. The forge bridge records the
first green run after the streak as `forge.green-run`; nobody else can
satisfy this stage, because the guard requires the bridge's signature.


---

# ci-failure / :resolved

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/ci-failure-resolved/


# ci-failure: resolved

The workflow is green again and the cause is on record. The stage is
sticky, so a later failure of the same workflow opens a new ticket for the
new streak instead of reopening this one.


---

# ci-failure / :triaged

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/ci-failure-triaged/


# ci-failure: triaged

The cause of the streak is on record. Whoever investigated it records one
of the declared causes:

- `tik set <id> cause=flaky` — the failure does not reproduce.
- `tik set <id> cause=code` — a change in this repository broke it.
- `tik set <id> cause=dependency` — an updated dependency broke it.
- `tik set <id> cause=config` — CI or build configuration broke it.
- `tik set <id> cause=infra` — runners, registries or the network failed.
- `tik set <id> cause=upstream` — a service outside our control failed.


---

# employee-onboarding: accounts

IT stands behind the account creation:
`tik set <id> accounts.email=<address>` signed by IT.
Runs in parallel with equipment — neither waits for the other.

# employee-onboarding / :equipped

# employee-onboarding: equipped

IT stands behind the hardware handover:
`tik set <id> equipment.ref=<asset tag>` signed by IT.

# employee-onboarding / :hired

# employee-onboarding: hired

The paperwork is real: a start date, the contract file, and HR's
signed reference to it.

- `tik set <id> start-date=2026-09-01`
- `tik attach <id> contract/<name>.pdf`
- HR records `tik set <id> contract.ref=<reference>` with their key.

# employee-onboarding / :ready

# employee-onboarding: ready

Both branches landed and a buddy is named:
`tik set <id> buddy=<name>`. Day one can happen.

# hypothesis / :captured

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/hypothesis-captured/


# Runbook: hypothesis / :captured

A belief worth testing exists. Capture it even half-formed — but do
not state it until you can also state what would kill it. A hypothesis
you cannot lose is marketing.


---

# hypothesis / :killed

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/hypothesis-killed/


# Runbook: hypothesis / :killed

Assert `verdict=:killed` and `evidence` of the kill: which criterion
fired, observed how. A kill is a RESULT — it retires a belief and
usually implies design work (the roadmap says what dies with it: kill
H1 and the core loop is wrong, not under-featured). Write the evidence
so the next design argument can cite it. Judgment stage, same rules as
:validated: sign reasoning a stranger could dispute.


---

# hypothesis / :running

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/hypothesis-running/


# Runbook: hypothesis / :running

Assert `experiment`: what is actually being run, on what, measured
how. If the full experiment cannot start yet, name the leg that can
and the leg that waits (H3 is the template). While running, record
datapoints as comments — negative ones ESPECIALLY; an experiment that
only logs good news is not running, it is performing.


---

# hypothesis / :stated

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/hypothesis-stated/


# Runbook: hypothesis / :stated

Assert `statement` (the falsifiable claim) and `kill` (what counts as
losing, decided NOW, before any work). Write the kill criterion as an
observable event, not a feeling: 'abandoned within a month', 'requires
prompt-side enforcement'. The process will not let a verdict through
without this — that is the point.


---

# hypothesis / :validated

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/hypothesis-validated/


# Runbook: hypothesis / :validated

Assert `verdict=:validated` and `evidence` that a stranger could
check: what ran, what was observed, why the kill criterion never
fired, and any scoping decisions that bound the claim. Sticky — later
doubts are a NEW hypothesis, not an edit. This stage is judgment:
the process cannot verify your evidence is sufficient, only that you
signed it. Leave enough that someone can dispute you specifically.


---

# identity-registry / :registry

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/identity-registry-registry/


<!--
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: The tik Authors
SPDX-License-Identifier: 0BSD
-->

# identity-registry: registry

The registry ticket accumulates signed `:identity` attestations, each
binding an IdP subject to an actor's public key. The ticket is always
in this stage — bindings are evidence, not workflow.

## Recording a binding

- `tik bridge oidc --registry <id> --actor <name>` runs the device-flow
  login and appends the binding, signed by the bridge's `TIK_KEY`.
- Rotation and re-attestation are newer attestations by the same
  bridge; readers take the latest binding per (issuer, subject).
- Revocation is a dispute of nothing — attestations are claims by the
  bridge; a binding the bridge no longer stands behind simply stops
  being re-attested, and lenses can require freshness via
  `:attested-within`.

## Reading bindings

`tik log <registry-id>` shows every binding with its signature;
`tik verify <registry-id>` checks them offline — no IdP call, ever.


---

# incident-response / :analyzed

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/incident-analyzed/


# incident-response: analyzed

The learning is written down.

- `tik set <id> root-cause=the actual cause, not the trigger`
- `tik set <id> postmortem.summary=a paragraph a stranger can learn from`


---

# incident-response / :declared

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/incident-declared/


# incident-response: declared

An incident exists once its severity and impact are on record.

- `tik set <id> severity=:sev1|:sev2|:sev3`
- `tik set <id> impact=who is affected and how`

Declare early and cheap — severity can be corrected later, and the
correction (like everything) is part of the record.


---

# incident-response / :mitigated

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/incident-mitigated/


# incident-response: mitigated

The bleeding has stopped, on the commander's word.

- The commander confirms severity by asserting it themselves —
  `tik set <id> severity=:sev1` signed with their key.
- `tik set <id> mitigation.note=what stopped the bleeding`


---

# incident-response / :postmortem-due

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/incident-postmortem-due/


# incident-response: postmortem-due

Five days have passed and no postmortem summary exists. Nobody set
this stage — time and absence derived it, and delivering the summary
(see analyzed) retracts it the same way.


---

# incident-response / :reviewed

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/incident-reviewed/


# incident-response: reviewed

A second pair of eyes accepted the analysis.

- Someone OTHER than the summary's author records
  `tik set <id> review.verdict=:accepted` — the commander signs it,
  and the definition enforces the different-person rule.


---

# okf-publish / :approved

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/okf-publish-approved/


# okf-publish · approved

An owner authorizes public release.

- A member of the `approver` role signs over `[:bundle]` — ideally a
  different person than the reviewer (separation of duties).
- Approval binds to the exact hash; revise the bundle and approval
  regresses, forcing re-approval before it can be published again.


---

# okf-publish / :drafted

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/okf-publish-drafted/


# okf-publish · drafted

The bundle exists and is identified.

- Attach the OKF bundle files under `okf/` (`tik attach <id> okf/...`).
- Record the bundle's content hash: `tik set <id> bundle=<sha256>`.
  This hash is what review and approval will sign over, so a later
  revision (new hash) automatically un-reviews the bundle.


---

# okf-publish / :published

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/okf-publish-published/


# okf-publish · published

The bundle is public.

- Record where it went live: `tik set <id> published.url=<url>`.
- This stage is NOT sticky: if the bundle is later revised, approval
  regresses and the ticket drops back out of `published` until the new
  version is re-reviewed and re-approved. Stale public knowledge
  un-publishes itself by derivation.


---

# okf-publish / :reviewed

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/okf-publish-reviewed/


# okf-publish · reviewed

A reviewer vouches the bundle is accurate.

- A member of the `reviewer` role signs over the `[:bundle]` fact
  (`tik sign <id> --over bundle`, or the review attestation flow).
- Reviewing a *different* hash than the current one does not count —
  the signature must cover the bundle as it stands now.


---

# release / :attested

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/release-attested/


<!--
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: The tik Authors
SPDX-License-Identifier: 0BSD
-->

# release: attested

The container image exists, an SBOM and build provenance were produced for it,
and the checksums carry a signature.

```sh
tik set <id> image=ghcr.io/metio/tik@sha256:... --actor ci
tik set <id> signature.bundle=<sha256 of SHA256SUMS.bundle> --actor ci
tik attest <id> :sbom --body '{:format "spdx-json" :digest "sha256:..."}' --actor ci
tik attest <id> :provenance --body '{:format "slsa-v1" :digest "sha256:..."}' --actor ci
```

The guard checks that a trusted attester said an SBOM exists. It does not read
the SBOM — guards never query anything, which is what keeps evaluation offline
and reproducible forever. The derivation is therefore exactly as trustworthy as
`:ci`, and that is a property to state plainly rather than bury.

Name the digest in the attestation body so a reader can fetch the document and
check it themselves.


---

# release / :built

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/release-built/


<!--
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: The tik Authors
SPDX-License-Identifier: 0BSD
-->

# release: built

The artifacts for this version exist and the pipeline has said which commit
produced them.

```sh
tik set <id> version=2026.8.5204821 commit=<sha> --actor ci
tik attach <id> checksums/SHA256SUMS
```

`commit` must be signed by a member of `:ci`: the pipeline is the only party
that can honestly say which source produced these bytes, and a human asserting
it is a claim about something they did not observe.

The checksums file is attached rather than pasted so it is addressed by its
hash. The hash is in the trust domain; the blob is not (ADR 0014). Anyone can
re-fetch the artifacts and check them against it without trusting this store.


---

# release / :published

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/release-published/


<!--
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: The tik Authors
SPDX-License-Identifier: 0BSD
-->

# release: published

A maintainer decided to ship, and that maintainer is not the party that built
it.

```sh
tik set <id> approval=:ship --actor seb
```

The `:different-person` guard compares who asserted `commit` with who asserted
`approval`. The pipeline cannot approve its own release — not because a rule
forbids it, but because the two facts would carry the same signature and the
guard would not hold.

Sticky milestone: shipping is a historical fact. A vulnerability disclosed next
week does not un-publish this version. It starts a new ticket, and this one
keeps saying what was true on the day.


---

# release / :scanned

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/release-scanned/


<!--
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: The tik Authors
SPDX-License-Identifier: 0BSD
-->

# release: scanned

A vulnerability scan ran against this version's dependencies, found nothing,
and said so recently enough to be about today's advisories.

```sh
tik attest <id> :vulnerability-scan --body '{:tool "clj-watson" :db "github-advisory"}' --actor ci
tik set <id> scan.result=:clean --actor ci
```

Both halves are needed and they say different things. The fact records the
verdict; the attestation records that a scan happened and when. The one-day
freshness window is what makes replay useless — a scan from last month is
cryptographically valid and fails this guard honestly, because the advisory
database it consulted no longer exists.

A scan that finds something is `scan.result=:findings`, which is not a failure
to record but a reason this version does not reach `:scanned`. Fix the finding
and cut a new version; do not re-assert the same value on this one.


---

# release / :withheld

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/release-withheld/


<!--
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: The tik Authors
SPDX-License-Identifier: 0BSD
-->

# release: withheld

A maintainer decided this version does not ship.

```sh
tik set <id> approval=:hold --actor seb
tik comment <id> "held: the scan is clean but the advisory for the transitive dep is unresolved upstream"
```

Recorded with the same weight as shipping, because the reason a version never
shipped is worth as much a year later as the reason one did — and it is the
question nobody can answer from a green pipeline.

Withholding is not terminal. A later `approval=:ship` supersedes it, and the
log keeps both decisions with their timestamps and signatures.


---

# renovate-migration / :configured

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/renovate-migration-configured/


# renovate-migration: configured

Renovate is in, Dependabot is out — the commits are the proof

## How a ticket gets here

- Record `renovate.config.ref`.
- Record `removal.commit`.


---

# renovate-migration / :planned

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/renovate-migration-planned/


# renovate-migration: planned

the approach is decided and on record

## How a ticket gets here

- Record `approach` — one of org-wide-config, repo-local-config.


---

# renovate-migration / :verified

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/renovate-migration-verified/


# renovate-migration: verified

Renovate demonstrably runs, and a maintainer stands behind the migration

## How a ticket gets here

- Record `renovate.dashboard`.
- Record `renovate.first-pr`.
- A member of the `maintainer` role records and signs their approval.


---

# supply-chain-release / :approved

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/supply-chain-release-approved/


# supply-chain-release · approved

Somebody who is not the pipeline looked at the evidence and decided to
ship.

- A member of `release-manager` records the decision:
  `tik set <id> approval=:ship`, signed with their own key.
- Four eyes is derived, not promised: `[:different-person [:commit]
  [:approval]]` compares who asserted each fact, so the actor that
  signed the commit cannot also sign the approval. A single-person
  project never reaches this stage, and the honest reading of that is
  "nobody independent looked", which is worth knowing.
- The stage is sticky. An advisory published next week does not
  un-approve a version that already shipped; it starts a new ticket
  against the next one.

Approve after `:attested` and `:scanned` hold, since both are the
material the decision is supposed to rest on. If you find yourself
approving first, the process is telling you something true about how
releases actually happen here.


---

# supply-chain-release / :attested

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/supply-chain-release-attested/


# supply-chain-release · attested

What the artifact is made of, and how it came to be — each said by a
party the registry trusts, each recent enough to be about this build.

- Record the artifact's digest and have `ci` sign it:
  `tik set <id> artifact.digest="\"sha256:…\""`.
- Bring the SBOM and the provenance in as attestations. If your pipeline
  already emits in-toto or SLSA documents, `tik bridge intoto <file>`
  maps their `predicateType` onto the claim these guards read, so no
  format is invented and nothing is transcribed by hand.
- Both windows are one day. An attestation older than that describes a
  different build, and the stage will not hold — re-attest as part of
  the release rather than replaying an older document.

tik checks that a trusted attester said these things. It does not read
the SBOM and forms no opinion about its contents, so this stage is worth
exactly what the attester is worth. Choose who may sign accordingly, and
say so to whoever reads the badge.


---

# supply-chain-release / :built

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/supply-chain-release-built/


# supply-chain-release · built

The pipeline says which commit produced these bytes, and hands over the
checksums that name them.

- Record the version and the commit from the pipeline's own context:
  `tik set <id> version="\"1.4.0\"" commit="\"$GITHUB_SHA\""`.
- The `commit` fact must be signed by a member of the `ci` role. A build
  is the one party that can honestly say which source produced which
  artifact, so a human asserting it proves nothing.
- Attach the checksums file under a `checksums/` prefix:
  `tik attach <id> dist/SHA256SUMS --as checksums/SHA256SUMS`. The
  artifact's hash is on the log; the blob is stored beside it, so a
  reader compares their download against a value the signature covers.

Give `ci` an ephemeral key bound to the pipeline's own workload identity
rather than a long-lived secret — `tik bridge workload --github` binds a
per-run keypair to the token the platform already issues, and nothing
long-lived exists to leak.

Name the subject that may bind `ci` under `:bindings` in `oidc.edn`
(ADR 0026) — `repo:<org>/<repo>:ref:refs/heads/main` for a workflow on
the default branch. Every repository on the platform can obtain a token
from the same issuer, so without that line any of them could bind `ci`.


---

# supply-chain-release / :scanned

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/supply-chain-release-scanned/


# supply-chain-release · scanned

A vulnerability scan ran against this build and came back clean.

- Attest the scan, naming the tool and the advisory database it read:
  `tik attest <id> :vulnerability-scan --body '{:tool "…" :db "…"}'`.
- Record the outcome as a fact `ci` signs:
  `tik set <id> scan.result=:clean` — or `:findings`.
- `:findings` is a legitimate answer and belongs on the record. Let the
  scan write what it found and let the ticket carry it; the stage stays
  unreached, and the release is a decision somebody makes with that in
  front of them.

Run the scan inside the release job rather than reusing an earlier
result. The one-day window exists because a scan is a claim about the
advisory database at a moment: last week's clean result is
cryptographically valid, honestly stale, and says nothing about the
advisories published since.


---

# supply-chain-release / :withheld

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/supply-chain-release-withheld/


# supply-chain-release · withheld

A version that was built and then deliberately not shipped, with the
decision and its author on the record.

- A member of `release-manager` records the hold:
  `tik set <id> approval=:hold`, signed.
- Say why in the same breath: `tik comment <id> "held: the scan found
  CVE-… in a transitive dependency"`. The comment is an artifact
  addressed by hash, so the reason travels in the evidence bundle
  alongside the decision.

This stage earns its keep months later. A version that quietly never
shipped looks identical to one nobody got around to, and the difference
matters when somebody asks what happened to 1.4.0. Reaching `:withheld`
answers that from the log rather than from memory.

A held version stays held. If the problem is fixed, that is a new build,
a new commit and a new ticket — not an edit to this one.


---

# support-request / :closed

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/support-request-closed/


# Runbook: support-request / :closed

Sticky milestone: only the customer's acknowledgement closes, and a
later retraction will NOT reopen (the log shows both truths). Ask for
the ack explicitly — the customer information-request pattern. If the
customer goes silent, the ticket honestly stays at :resolved; do not
assert the ack on their behalf, ever (authorship is the whole point,
ADR 0010).


---

# support-request / :escalated

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/support-request-escalated/


# Runbook: support-request / :escalated

This stage derives on its own: 48 hours without a category. There is
no action that produces it — the runbook is for reacting to it. An
escalated ticket means triage is the bottleneck: find why (nobody on
rotation? report unintelligible?) and either triage it now or record
what blocks triage. Escalation clears itself the moment a category
lands (fact-level negation).


---

# support-request / :received

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/support-request-received/


# Runbook: support-request / :received

A new report exists; nothing is known yet. Read the title and any
attached artifacts. Your job is to move it toward triage: get a
category and a severity asserted by a triager. If the report is
unintelligible, ask the reporter (a comment or an information-request
effect) rather than guessing a category — a wrong category asserted
confidently is worse than an honest gap.


---

# support-request / :reproducible

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/support-request-reproducible/


# Runbook: support-request / :reproducible

Attach a reproduction under `repro/` — a script, a request trace, a
recording; the smallest artifact that makes the failure happen again.
If you cannot reproduce it, say so in a comment with what you tried;
do not attach a placeholder to satisfy the guard (evidence theater,
PLAN §18). A technical ticket without a repro simply is not resolvable
yet — that is the process being honest, not slow.


---

# support-request / :resolved

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/support-request-resolved/


# Runbook: support-request / :resolved

Assert `resolution.ref` pointing at the fix (commit, config change,
knowledge-base answer). For technical tickets the reproduction must
exist first — 'fixed it but can't show the bug' does not resolve.
Resolution is a claim the customer has not yet accepted; do not
consider the work done here.


---

# support-request / :triaged

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/support-request-triaged/


# Runbook: support-request / :triaged

Assert `category` and `severity` — both must come from a triager
(the `:signed-by` guard checks the role, not the values). Category is
a claim about what KIND of problem this is; when genuinely unsure,
pick the closest and say why in a comment — a later dispute is cheap
and leaves better history than stalling. Severity reflects impact on
the customer, not effort to fix.


---

# tik-dev / :captured

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/tik-dev-captured/


# Runbook: tik-dev / :captured

A thought exists; the ticket preserves it. Give it a title that will
mean something in six months. Nothing else is required — capture must
stay cheap or ideas stop being written down. Move to triage when you
can honestly write one summary sentence and name the kind.


---

# tik-dev / :implemented

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/tik-dev-implemented/


# Runbook: tik-dev / :implemented

Assert `commit` naming the commit that does the work. The commit must
exist before the fact does — the fact is a claim about evidence, and
the evidence is the git history. One feature, one commit, stacked on
main (this repo's workflow).


---

# tik-dev / :landed

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/tik-dev-landed/


# Runbook: tik-dev / :landed

Assert `gate=:green` only after the FULL local gate: kaocha, kondo
(0/0), eastwood, splint, cljfmt, tla, process tests, reuse, typos,
markdown. Not the one check your change touched — all of them.
Sticky: a later gate dispute does not un-land; file a new bug ticket
instead. If the gate is red, assert `gate=:red` honestly and fix
forward.


---

# tik-dev / :parked

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/tik-dev-parked/


# Runbook: tik-dev / :parked

Assert `parked.reason` — the reason is the deliverable. Cite the
verdict that parks it (a PLAN §19 entry, a trigger condition not yet
met). Parked is not closed: the ticket stays visible on the board and
can resume by simply asserting the missing facts. Parking without a
real reason is deferral theater.


---

# tik-dev / :triaged

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/tik-dev-triaged/


# Runbook: tik-dev / :triaged

Assert `summary` (what and why, one breath) and `kind`
(feature/bug/docs/spike) as a maintainer. If it duplicates existing
work, link it (`link.duplicate-of=<uuid>`) instead of triaging twice.
If it should wait, this is also where you park it — with the reason,
not silently.


---

# track / :done

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/track-done/


<!--
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: The tik Authors
SPDX-License-Identifier: 0BSD
-->

# track: done

The thing ended — say how:

```sh
tik set <id> outcome="shipped in v2; see order #1234"
```

A few honest words beat a closed flag: the outcome is the only thing
anyone will want from this ticket in a year.


---

# track / :open

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/runbooks/track-open/


<!--
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: The tik Authors
SPDX-License-Identifier: 0BSD
-->

# track: open

The ticket exists. There is no workflow to satisfy — record what is
true as it happens:

- `tik set <id> key=value` for facts worth keeping.
- `tik comment <id> <text>` for anything else.
- `tik attach <id> <file>` for evidence.

When several track tickets start following the same informal shape,
run `tik author` and give that shape a real definition.


---

# Decisions

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/decisions/


Every load-bearing choice in tik has a record: the decision, the context that
forced it, and the consequences that follow. Several exist to name something
tik will *not* do, which is the part that keeps the model small.

New here, read these four: [derived state is never
authoritative](/decisions/0013-derived-state-never-authoritative/) is the one
law written as a constraint on every future feature;
[coordination-free](/decisions/0021-coordination-free-horizontal-scaling/) is
its companion; [stored bytes are the hashed
region](/decisions/0007-stored-bytes-are-the-hashed-region/) is why
`sha256sum` alone audits a store; and [three
clocks](/decisions/0012-time-semantics/) is why a guard's meaning includes
which clock it reads.

These files live in the repository's knowledge bundle under `kb/decisions/`,
so a checkout and this site carry the same record.

## The laws

| Decision | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| [0013](/decisions/0013-derived-state-never-authoritative/) | Derived material may be cached only if disposable and untrusted. |
| [0021](/decisions/0021-coordination-free-horizontal-scaling/) | No leader, no lock, no consensus — on any correctness path. |
| [0001](/decisions/0001-event-log-acceptance-test/) | The event-log acceptance test every feature must pass. |

## Derivation

| Decision | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| [0005](/decisions/0005-stratified-negation/) | Negation inside the fixpoint must be stratified to stay deterministic. |
| [0003](/decisions/0003-conflicts-block/) | Concurrent conflicting assertions block guards; people resolve them. |
| [0016](/decisions/0016-explain-stability-contract/) | Explain's structured reasons are the stable API; the prose is not. |
| [0018](/decisions/0018-conformance/) | Conformance is the corpus, the laws, and the normative sweep semantics. |
| [0019](/decisions/0019-effects-observe-derivation/) | Effects observe derivation; transport is not a domain concept. |
| [0030](/decisions/0030-a-notebook-enters-a-ticket-through-a-probe/) | What a kajero notebook knows about a ticket enters it through a probe, as facts its guards read like any other. |

## Time

| Decision | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| [0012](/decisions/0012-time-semantics/) | Three clocks, never conflated; the clock is part of the guard. |
| [0022](/decisions/0022-no-step-reads-the-future/) | The claimed clock is clamped to the evaluated clock. |

## The log and its bytes

| Decision | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| [0004](/decisions/0004-mandatory-parents/) | Parents are mandatory; the log is a Merkle DAG. |
| [0006](/decisions/0006-hash-policy/) | SHA-256, self-describing ids, one algorithm per store. |
| [0007](/decisions/0007-stored-bytes-are-the-hashed-region/) | Stored bytes are exactly the hashed region; signatures are detached. |
| [0008](/decisions/0008-canonical-serialization-protocol/) | Canonical serialization is a versioned wire protocol. |
| [0017](/decisions/0017-deletion-and-compaction/) | Events are never deleted; blobs may be; nothing compacts into authority. |
| [0020](/decisions/0020-eventstore-contract/) | The contract every storage backend must honour. |

## Trust and authority

| Decision | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| [0010](/decisions/0010-authority-model/) | Signatures establish authorship; authorization is derived. |
| [0011](/decisions/0011-log-admission-vs-trust/) | The log admits all well-formed claims; trust is evaluated, not filtered. |
| [0009](/decisions/0009-unknown-data-policy/) | Unknown data is handled differently per layer, on purpose. |
| [0014](/decisions/0014-artifact-semantics/) | The artifact hash is in the trust domain; the blob is not. |
| [0015](/decisions/0015-process-definition-trust/) | Definition hash is identity; publication signatures are authority. |
| [0002](/decisions/0002-pinned-process-versions/) | Tickets pin their definition hash; migration is an event. |
| [0023](/decisions/0023-key-bindings-are-evidence/) | A verified key binding grants signing authority; pinned keys anchor it. |
| [0024](/decisions/0024-link-values-name-foreign-tickets/) | A link's value names its referent; a foreign ticket carries the head observed. |
| [0025](/decisions/0025-the-evidence-bundle-is-a-versioned-format/) | The evidence bundle is a named, versioned format; a badge names the derivation. |
| [0026](/decisions/0026-a-binding-policy-names-who-may-bind-which-actor/) | A binding policy names which subject may bind which actor; a bound key speaks only while its token was live. |
| [0031](/decisions/0031-a-pipeline-is-a-ticket-that-lives-only-in-its-bundle/) | A pipeline run is one ticket in a throwaway store, its jobs bind their own keys, and the bundle it publishes is the only record. |
| [0032](/decisions/0032-the-sticky-carry-enters-by-stratum/) | Guards read the sticky carry from the first sweep, and :after admits a carried stage only in its own stratum. |
| [0033](/decisions/0033-a-stratum-counts-every-wait/) | A negated stage must enter for good before its negator is first judged, counting every stage reference it waits on and every negation parity. |
| [0034](/decisions/0034-a-rollout-subject-need-not-be-a-git-repository/) | A rollout takes its members from a declared population, and a subject needs no git repository. |
| [0035](/decisions/0035-a-binding-token-commits-to-its-key/) | A binding counts only when its token names the key it binds, through its nonce or an audience suffix. |
| [0036](/decisions/0036-post-quantum-signatures-are-hybrid/) | Post-quantum signatures arrive as a hybrid ML-DSA-65 sidecar beside SSHSIG, with a store policy, a witness anchor, and the content hash as a parameter of the format version. |
| [0038](/decisions/0038-one-shared-server-holds-no-keys/) | One shared server per organisation holds no signing keys; agents sign their own events, prove their actor per connection, and receive work through roles. |
| [0037](/decisions/0037-a-batch-review-is-a-scoped-delegation/) | One signature approves a reviewed batch, through a delegation scoped to the shown heads and the verdict fact, valid for at most five minutes. |
| [0039](/decisions/0039-the-role-register-is-a-signed-log/) | Proposed: the role register is a log of edits signed by authorities its genesis names by key, and a role a definition reserves for humans refuses agent actors. |
| [0040](/decisions/0040-a-notifier-pushes-hints-not-evidence/) | Proposed: a local notifier pushes hints of verified stage changes to subscribers on a private Unix socket, never evidence. |
| [0041](/decisions/0041-one-backend-serves-several-stores-each-in-its-own-context/) | Proposed: one backend serves several stores, each in its own context with its own key, actor, actors file, board and MCP token, and refuses to start when any store fails to open. |
| [0042](/decisions/0042-a-multi-store-backend-runs-each-pipeline-as-a-child-process/) | Proposed: a multi-store backend runs each pipeline as a child process on a grid with jitter, never overlapping, bounded and reported, and watches mailboxes only with DKIM at a pinned verifier and TLS that names the host. |
| [0043](/decisions/0043-a-mail-reporter-is-a-keyed-pseudonym/) | Proposed: the mail bridge records a DKIM-authenticated sender of a new ticket as a keyed HMAC pseudonym, keeps the address in a private table outside the store that an erasure request empties, and refuses blocked senders before writing anything. |
| [0044](/decisions/0044-a-library-reads-one-ticket-and-never-writes/) | Proposed: `tik.api` reads, verifies and derives one ticket in process, read-only, without starting a process, with the ladder `tik verify` runs. |
| [0027](/decisions/0027-a-pinned-issuer-key-is-its-kid-and-its-material/) | A pinned issuer key is identified by its kid and its key material; a reused kid keeps both keys. |
| [0028](/decisions/0028-a-spiffe-jwt-svid-binds-like-an-oidc-token/) | A SPIFFE JWT-SVID binds like an OIDC token; its trust domain is its issuer. |
| [0029](/decisions/0029-relations-are-events-no-stage-reads/) | A relation between tickets is its own event kind, with a closed vocabulary that no stage reads. |

# tik.api reads, verifies and derives one ticket of a store in process, never writes, and judges signatures with the code tik verify runs

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/decisions/0044-a-library-reads-one-ticket-and-never-writes/


# ADR 0044: A library reads one ticket and never writes

## Decision

Proposed on 2026-11-28. Not accepted. It is implemented in `cli/tik/api.clj`
under ticket f106aa78 of the metio store. Each choice names the
alternatives, ranked by security first, then reuse, then performance.

**`tik.api` is the one namespace another program calls to read tik
evidence in process: `open-store`, `resolve-id`, `ticket`, `derive` and
`verify-ticket`, versioned by `tik.api/version` (1).** kajero checks
`tik:<id>` evidence with it instead of starting `tik status <id> --edn`
per ticket. The contract is the namespace docstring; this record says why
it has that shape.

1. **One ladder for the CLI and the library.** The per-ticket verify
   ladder moved out of `tik.audit` into `tik.verify/ticket-ladder`, which
   returns items (`:section`, `:check`, `:note`, `:skip`) instead of
   printing. `tik verify` prints `tik.verify/line` of each item, so its
   output is unchanged byte for byte, and `tik.api/verify-ticket` returns
   the items. The definition checks moved the same way
   (`tik.verify/definition-items`). Rejected: a second, library-only
   verifier, which would drift from the audit, and a verifier that parses
   the CLI's printed lines.

2. **Read-only by construction.** The handle's store refuses `append!`
   and `put-sidecar!` with `:tik.api/read-only`; a SQLite store is opened
   through an SQLite URI with `mode=ro`, so the connection itself can
   neither create the file, create a table nor change a row; nothing
   materializes the built-in track definition into `processes/` as the
   CLI does; and no derived-state cache is written.
   `tik.identity-trust/signer-view` returns allowed-signers text instead
   of writing a temporary file per set of granted keys. Rejected: relying
   on callers not to call writers, and opening SQLite read-write and
   promising not to write.

3. **No process, no network.** `tik.sign/*ssh-keygen-fallback*` is bound
   false for every library call. A signature by a key type tik.sshsig does
   not read (RSA, ECDSA) is then `:unchecked`, and its check fails where
   `tik verify` would ask ssh-keygen and might pass. The library is
   therefore stricter than the CLI for those keys and never weaker. The
   binding is read before the availability probe, which itself starts
   ssh-keygen. Rejected: allowing the fallback behind an option, because a
   library user that needs RSA keys can run `tik verify`, and an option
   is one more way to start a process from a long-running server.

4. **Bounds before reads.** Every call measures a ticket before reading
   it: event and sidecar sizes, the event count, the ticket's total bytes
   (`stat` per file for the file store, one `length(bytes)` query for
   SQLite), and refuses a symbolic link or anything that is not a regular
   file in a ticket directory, since its size says nothing about what
   reading it returns (`/dev/zero`). The config files the ladder reads
   whole (`actors`, `pq-signers`, `signatures.edn`, `oidc.edn`,
   `roles.edn`, `jwks/`) and definition files are bounded too. The
   defaults are in `tik.api/default-limits`; `open-store` takes lower or
   higher ones. Rejected: trusting the store reader, which bounds nesting
   depth but not size.

5. **The pinned definition, or a refusal.** `derive` refuses with
   `:tik.api/definition-mismatch` when the definition it finds does not
   hash to the ticket's pin. `tik status` derives under the named file
   with a warning on stderr in that case; a library caller would not see
   the warning. `{:allow-unpinned-definition true}` derives as status
   does, and `:definition` names the hash used.

6. **Ticket references.** A uuid, the full id, or a prefix of at least 8
   characters naming exactly one ticket; an ambiguous prefix is refused
   with its `:candidates`. Rejected: tik's CLI rule of any non-blank
   prefix, because a short prefix stored in another system's record
   silently starts naming a different ticket when the store grows.

7. **Stable refusals.** Every refusal is an ex-info with a `:type` in the
   `tik.api` namespace; store and parse failures become
   `:tik.api/unreadable`, derivation failures `:tik.api/underivable`.

8. **Small load.** Requiring `tik.api` loads 25 tik namespaces (the
   kernel, the stores, signature and identity verification) plus malli,
   and none of the CLI, MCP, bridges or HTTP code (measured with
   `all-ns` on the JVM and babashka: requiring `tik.cli` on top loads 58
   more namespaces). cheshire is resolved only when an identity binding
   must be verified, and the SQLite driver only for a SQLite store, so a
   native image that needs either requires `cheshire.core` or
   `tik.store.sqlite-jdbc` at build time, as `tik.main` does.

## Consequences

- The equivalence of `derive` with `tik status --edn` and of
  `verify-ticket` with `tik verify` is a test over every ticket of the
  corpus stores, a copy of the repository's own store and built file and
  SQLite stores (`test/tik/api_test.clj`).
- A change to the ladder changes the CLI and the library together; a
  change to what `tik.api` returns that removes or renames a documented
  key bumps `tik.api/version`.
- The library verifies one ticket and its pinned definition. The
  store-level checks of a whole-store `tik verify` (every archived
  definition, roots, identity binding health) stay in the CLI.


---

# A local notifier pushes hints of verified stage changes to subscribers on a private Unix socket, and never evidence

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/decisions/0040-a-notifier-pushes-hints-not-evidence/


# ADR 0040: A notifier pushes hints, not evidence

## Decision

Proposed on 2026-11-27. Not accepted. It is implemented as
`tik notify`, under ticket 19030002 of the metio store. Each choice
below names the alternatives and why it was taken, ranked by security
first, then extensibility and re-use, then performance.

**`tik notify` watches one or more local stores. It re-derives and
verifies every ticket whose log changed, and pushes a hint of each
change of its current stages to the local subscribers that asked for
that ticket.** A hint names the store, the ticket, its title, the
stages it left and entered, and the actor of the event that moved it.
It carries nothing else. The receiver treats it as a reason to look,
and re-derives with `tik status` before acting.

1. **Hints only.** The payload is exactly the keys `store`, `ticket`,
   `title`, `from`, `to` and `actor` (`tik.notify/hint-keys`). It holds
   no fact values and no instructions. A fact can hold a customer's
   data or text written to steer an agent, and a hint goes into a
   model's context. The title and the actor are folded to one line of at
   most 160 and 64 characters, with control, format and bidi-override
   characters dropped. That keeps a title from forging a second JSON
   line or reordering what a terminal shows. The alternative, a payload
   carrying the facts that moved the ticket, was declined: it would turn
   the notifier into a second read path that bypasses whatever a reader
   may see. It would also make the hint look like evidence, which the
   three-questions law (PLAN §12) reserves for derivation.

2. **Re-derived and verified.** The notifier never trusts an event
   because it arrived. For every ticket whose fingerprint moved, it
   derives the ticket from the store with the same functions `tik ls`
   uses, then requires three things:
   - the store has an actors registry;
   - every event the cursor had not seen carries a signature;
   - the whole verify ladder over the ticket passes: L0 integrity, the
     DAG, every signature present, and the signature policy.

   A ticket that fails sends nothing and logs why. Its cursor entry
   keeps the last verified stages, so the next verified change diffs
   against stages that were verified. Taking stage changes from a
   stream of incoming events was declined, because it would believe an
   event before `verify` does.

3. **Local only.**
   - **Socket.** Subscribers connect to a Unix socket in a directory
     the notifier creates `rwx------`, or refuses when it exists with
     another owner or wider permissions. The socket itself is
     `rw-------`.
   - **Peer check.** Every accepted connection's kernel peer credentials
     (`SO_PEERCRED`) must name the notifier's own user. A peer the
     platform cannot name is refused.
   - **No network.** There is no network listener. Delivery to another
     host stays with the effects bridge (ADR 0019) or a future
     notifier that runs inside the shared server (ADR 0038).
   - **Alternatives declined.** A loopback HTTP endpoint would reach
     every local user and every web page that can rebind DNS. A
     desktop bus would tie the notifier to one desktop.

4. **Store-aware.** A subscription names one store. It is admitted
   only when that store's root directory belongs to the subscriber's
   user, the same test the operating system applies to reading the
   store itself. A notifier configured with several stores
   (`notify.edn` `:stores`) never tells a subscriber of one store about
   another. Today that boundary is the operating-system user. Once
   connections carry the signed actor assertion of ADR 0038 point 4,
   the admission check is the place to require that the actor may read
   the store. That is how one organisation's session stays out of
   another organisation's tickets on a shared machine.

5. **Coalesced and rate-limited.** Diffs wait in a coalescer keyed by
   store and ticket for a window (5 s by default). A ticket pending in
   the window keeps the stages it started from and takes the newest
   stages, title and actor, so a burst of events gives one hint per
   ticket per window. A ticket that came back to where it started gives
   none. Each subscriber has a token bucket (10 hints, one more every
   6 s by default). Past it, hints are dropped and logged, never
   queued without bound.

6. **Idempotent across restarts.** A cursor records, per store and
   ticket, the fingerprint, the events and the stages last acted on. It
   is written atomically under `$XDG_STATE_HOME/tik/notify/` whenever it
   moves, and a restart diffs against it. The cursor is disposable
   porcelain (ADR 0013). Losing it costs one silent baseline. It never
   costs a replay of old hints, because a first start records the
   stores without reporting them. Delivery is therefore at most once.
   That is the right failure for a hint, where ADR 0019's effects choose
   at least once for messages that must arrive.

7. **Pluggable delivery.** A sink is one protocol method,
   `deliver!`, returning whether it is still there. Three sinks ship:
   - a socket subscriber;
   - a configured command, run without a shell with `{ticket}`,
     `{title}`, `{line}` and the other placeholders substituted as
     whole arguments. `notify-send` gives a desktop notification this
     way.
   - a fake one, in the tests.

   Two subscribers ship as verbs:
   - `tik notify watch` prints one JSON line per hint.
   - `tik notify channel` is a stdio MCP server that forwards hints as
     Claude Code channel events.

8. **How a hint reaches a Claude Code session.** This was checked
   against the MCP 2026-07-28 specification, the Claude Code
   documentation and the strings of Claude Code 2.1.331 on 2026-11-27.
   In order of preference:
   - **The Monitor tool running `tik notify watch`.** Claude Code
     documents Monitor as generally available. It "runs a command in
     the background and feeds each output line back to Claude", under
     the session's Bash permission rules. It needs nothing beyond the
     notifier.
   - **A channel.** Claude Code registers `tik notify channel` as a
     channel when the session starts with
     `--dangerously-load-development-channels server:<name>`. Channels
     are a research preview, work over stdio only, and are not
     registered on revision 2026-07-28. The bridge therefore speaks only
     the legacy `initialize` handshake and answers `server/discover`
     with -32601. It reads each stdin line within the 1 MiB limit of
     `tik mcp`, holding at most that much of a line: a longer line, or
     one briko.json refuses, answers -32700 with a null id and the rule
     in `data.rule`, and the next line is read.
   - **MCP resource subscriptions: blocked.** Under 2026-07-28 a client
     must request `resourceSubscriptions` on `subscriptions/listen`
     before a server may send `notifications/resources/updated`.
     Claude Code 2.1.331 requests only the three `list_changed` kinds,
     and in the legacy era registers no handler for resource updates.
   - **The `cc-socks` inbox socket: declined.** Its message format is
     undocumented. The documented auth line serves a session's own
     child processes.

9. **One backend, later.** The verb runs as its own process today. It
   is shaped to become a continuous `tik backend` pipeline
   (`{:id :notify :watch true :run ["notify" "--config" "…"]}`), and the
   one-backend-many-stores plan reuses the multi-store loop directly.
   The CLI's store root became bindable for that (`tik.cli-core/*root*`),
   so one process derives each store in turn under its own root.

## Context

Agents and the maintainer learned about ticket changes by polling: an
hourly request check, plus `SendMessage` pings between the metio and
infra.run sessions written by hand. The kajero idea 25d4b7d4 proposed a
local notifier that finds the right session and pushes the change
instead, under the law that the notifier must never become a source of
truth.

The effects bridge (ADR 0019) already observes derivation and fires
outbound sinks. It answers a different question, at a different
latency:

- **What it reports.** Effects report every stage a ticket reaches,
  once per (ticket, stage, sink). A hint reports where the ticket is
  now, relative to where it was.
- **When it runs.** Effects run in batches, from a pipeline. A hint
  runs live.
- **Who it reaches.** Effects deliver at least once to sinks configured
  in advance. Hints go at most once to subscribers that come and go
  with their sessions.

Folding the notifier into effects would weaken both: effects would
gain subscriptions and a socket, and hints would gain a ledger keyed on
reached stages that cannot express "moved back".

## Consequences

- A session can replace a polling loop with `tik notify watch` under
  Monitor, plus a slow fallback poll for anything missed while it was
  not subscribed.
- Time alone can move a ticket, through `:elapsed-since` guards.
  Without an event there is no fingerprint change, so the notifier does
  not report such a move. The fallback poll covers it.
- The fingerprint reads names, not bytes. A signature replaced in place
  under the same name is judged at the next real change, and `tik
  verify` remains the audit.
- A write appends its event before its signature sidecar. A poll that
  falls between the two logs a refusal for the unsigned event; the
  sidecar then changes the fingerprint, and the next poll verifies the
  ticket and sends the hint.
- Several notifiers on one estate do not coordinate. Each keeps its own
  cursor and socket, which ADR 0021 permits for delivery. A user runs
  one per machine.

## Alternatives considered

- **Push stage changes through MCP resource subscriptions on the
  existing tik MCP server.** Blocked today; see point 8.
- **Write into Claude Code's per-session sockets.** Declined; see point
  8.
- **inotify instead of a poll.** The poll lists each ticket's event
  directory every 2 s, which is cheap at the store sizes in use and
  works the same on the SQLite store. A watcher can replace the poll
  without touching anything above `fingerprints`.
- **Deliver to every subscriber of a store without selectors.** Each
  subscription carries a `tik ls --where` selector instead, evaluated on
  the ticket's fresh derivation, so a session hears only about the
  tickets it asked for.


---

# A multi-store backend runs each pipeline as a child process of the same binary, scheduled on a grid with jitter, never overlapping, bounded and reported, and watches mailboxes under strict rules

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/decisions/0042-a-multi-store-backend-runs-each-pipeline-as-a-child-process/


# ADR 0042: A multi-store backend runs each pipeline as a child process

## Decision

Proposed on 2026-11-27. Not accepted. It is implemented in `tik backend`
under ticket 7eb48e71 of the metio store, and builds on ADR 0041. Each
choice names the alternatives and why it was taken, ranked by security
first, then extensibility and re-use, then performance.

**A multi-store backend (a config with `:stores`) runs every run of every
pipeline as a child process of the same tik binary, started with its
store's variables only. The pipelines replace the systemd timers that ran
one bridge each: they fire on a grid with jitter, collapse missed fires
into one, never overlap a pipeline's own runs, are killed when they
outlive a timeout, write labelled lines to the journal and send a failure
report.** A single-store backend (`pipelines.edn` without `:stores`) is
unchanged and still runs its verbs in process.

```clojure
{:stores {:metio {:root "~/git/github.com/metio/.tik" :org "metio" :actor "claude"
                  :key {:command ["pasejo" "secret" "show" "--store" "personal-ls" "tik/metio/claude"]}}}
 :on-failure {:run ["notify-send" "--urgency=critical" "tik {store}/{pipeline}" "{reason}"]}
 :pipelines [{:id :github-metio :store :metio :every "PT10M" :as "github"
              :key {:credential "github-metio-key"} :run ["bridge" "github"]}
             {:id :mail-metio :store :metio :watch true :as "mail"
              :key {:credential "mail-metio-key"} :config "imap.edn"
              :run ["bridge" "imap" "--watch"]}]}
```

### 1. A run is a child process, not a call

Each run is `<this tik> <verb> --actor <as> [--config <file>]` with the
environment of `tik.context/child-env` for its store: `TIK_ROOT`,
`TIK_KEY` and `TIK_ACTOR` of that store and pipeline, nothing of any
other store's.

- **Security.** A child shares no memory with another store's runs. The
  derived-row cache leak found under ADR 0041 shows the class of bug a
  shared process invites: any process-global cache, rate limiter or
  `alter-var-root` is a channel between stores. A process boundary closes
  every such channel at once, where a context binding closes only the ones
  somebody remembered to bind. The boundary is against mistakes: every
  child runs as the same Unix user, so a compromised child could read any
  file the backend can.
- **A bounded run needs a kill.** A bridge blocked in a socket read ignores
  `Thread.interrupt`, so an in-process run cannot be stopped when it hangs.
  A child is stopped with SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after five seconds, with
  the processes it started (a password manager, an ssh tunnel) where the
  runtime can list them (the JVM and the native image; babashka cannot).
- **Labelled output.** A child's stdout and stderr are read line by line
  and written as `[store/pipeline] <line>`, from every thread the verb
  starts. An in-process run captures only the calling thread's `*out*`, and
  only once the run ends.
- **Cost.** One process start per run: milliseconds for the native binary,
  about a second for babashka. A ten-minute bridge interval does not
  notice either.

Rejected: in-process runs bound to the store context (ADR 0041's first
shape), for the reasons above.

### 2. How the backend names itself

`:exec` in the config wins. Without it, a native image runs its own
executable (`/proc/self/exe`) and babashka runs `bb --config <its bb.edn>
tik`. Any other runtime, such as a JVM REPL, cannot name its own command
line, and the backend refuses to start pipelines rather than guess. The
`javax.net.ssl.trustStore*` properties the backend was started with are
passed on as `-D` arguments, so a private CA reaches every run.

### 3. The scheduler is pure

`tik.schedule` takes the clock and the random draw as arguments and
returns data; `tik.pipeline-run` executes its decisions. The properties are
property-tested without a clock or a process.

- **Grid and jitter.** A pipeline keeps a grid point (start plus whole
  intervals) and fires at the grid point plus a draw from `[0, :jitter)`.
  The default jitter is one minute, the timers' `RandomizedDelaySec=60`,
  and never more than half the interval. A grid does not drift by the run
  time, as an `OnCalendar` timer does not.
- **Catch-up.** Every fire missed while the backend was stopped or the
  machine slept collapses into one run (`Persistent=true`). A sleep does
  not advance during a suspend, so the scheduler re-reads the wall clock at
  least every 30 seconds. A fire found more than 35 seconds late is
  re-drawn into its jitter window once, so the pipelines that all missed
  do not start in the same instant after a resume.
- **No overlap.** A pipeline due while its run still goes is not started a
  second time; the fire is skipped, logged, and the next one is the next
  grid point. Different pipelines run concurrently. This is a per-process
  guard on delivery timing, not a lock on any correctness path: two
  backends running the same pipeline still converge, because the verbs
  mint content-addressed events (ADR 0021).
- **Bounded.** A run is killed after `:timeout`, by default its interval,
  so a stuck run never outlives the period it belongs to.
- **Restarts.** A `:watch` pipeline restarts after 1 s, doubling to 60 s
  while it keeps failing fast, and starts over at 1 s once a run lasted a
  minute.

### 4. Failure reports

`:on-failure {:run [...] :repeat "PT1H"}` runs a command without a shell
when a run fails or times out, with `{store}`, `{pipeline}`, `{exit}` and
`{reason}` filled in separate arguments. Every value comes from the
backend (names from its config, a number, a sentence it wrote), never from
a remote, and no output of the run is passed on. A pipeline is reported
when it goes from working to failing, and again after `:repeat` while it
keeps failing; `"PT0S"` reports every failure as systemd's `OnFailure=`
does. The default of an hour exists because a crash-looping watcher
restarts every minute. Every failure is also written as `FAILED: <reason>`
at priority err.

### 5. The journal

Every line is labelled `[store/pipeline]`. When systemd sets
`JOURNAL_STREAM`, each line also carries an sd-daemon priority prefix
(`<6>` progress, `<5>` a skip, `<4>` a run's stderr, `<3>` failures), so
`journalctl -p warning` shows what needs attention. Line breaks inside a
child's line are flattened, so a line cannot forge another pipeline's
label. A child never sees `JOURNAL_STREAM`, since it writes to a pipe.

### 6. Config files per pipeline

`:config` names the verb's config file, relative to the store's root,
absolute, or `~/…`; the backend passes it as `--config <absolute path>`
and refuses to start when it does not exist. `--config` inside `:run` is
refused, since it would resolve against the backend's working directory.
Without `:config` the verb reads its default file at the store's root, as
before.

### 7. Delegate keys

A pipeline's `:key` must sign as its `:as` in its own store's `actors`
file (ADR 0041). Two pipelines of stores with different organisations may
not resolve to the same key unless `:allow-shared-keys` names the pair,
which extends ADR 0041's rule from store keys to delegate keys: one
organisation's delegate never signs for another's.

The backend also refuses `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`,
`GITLAB_TOKEN`, `REDMINE_API_KEY` and `ODOO_PASSWORD` in its environment.
Every child inherits the backend's environment, so a token meant for one
organisation's bridge would reach every store's runs. The configs name
their secrets with `{:command …}` or `{:credential …}` instead.

### 8. Mailboxes

`bridge imap` reads one mailbox under `:imap` or a list under
`:mailboxes`, each with an `:id`, its own `:imap` settings and its own
`:process`; the other top-level keys are defaults for every mailbox. A
pipeline belongs to one store, so a store's mailboxes share one pipeline
and one process, each mailbox on its own connection and thread with its
own backoff. Adding `support@klimpi.app` is a list entry.

A `:mailboxes` list, and any IMAP pipeline of a multi-store backend
(checked before the backend starts), holds to strict rules:

- `:dkim {:require true :authserv-id …}` with a non-blank id, so a From is
  credited only when the pinned verifier stamped `dkim=pass` for its
  domain;
- the password is a `{:command …}`, `{:credential …}` or `{:file …}`
  spec, never a literal and never `{:env …}`, which every child inherits;
- the pipeline's key must sign as every actor a mailbox records mail as
  (`:default-actor` and each `:from->actor` value), or what it ingests
  would not verify.

For every IMAP and POP3 connection, strict or not: a TLS socket checks
that the certificate names the host (a raw `SSLSocket` checks only that
the chain is trusted, so any certificate a trusted CA issued for any name
was accepted), and plaintext (`:tls false`) is refused for any host not
written as a loopback address, judged on the text without DNS. A watch
that drops says why on stderr, without the password, and a plaintext
refusal ends it instead of retrying.

## Consequences

- The systemd timer per bridge and the board service become one unit
  running `tik backend --config backend.edn`; see the local-service guide.
- The board and MCP move below `/s/<store>/` (ADR 0041), so MCP clients
  registered on `/mcp` need the new path.
- `tik.process-tree` exists only for the JVM and the native image;
  babashka stops a timed-out run without its descendants.
- Not done: a per-mailbox fact on new tickets (such as `product=klimpi`);
  each mailbox chooses its process instead.


---

# One tik backend serves several stores, each in its own context with its own key, actor, actors file, board and MCP token

Source: https://tik.projects.metio.wtf/decisions/0041-one-backend-serves-several-stores-each-in-its-own-context/


# ADR 0041: One backend serves several stores, each in its own context

## Decision

Proposed on 2026-11-27. Not accepted. It is implemented in `tik
backend` under ticket 03ec81f1 of the metio store. Each choice below names
the alternatives and why it was taken, ranked by security first, then
extensibility and re-use, then performance.

**A `tik backend` whose config has `:stores` serves several stores from
one process. Every request, pipeline run and subprocess for a store runs
inside that store's context, and the context alone decides the root, the
signing key and the actor.** A single-store invocation (`pipelines.edn`
without `:stores`, `tik serve`, `tik mcp`, every other verb) is
unchanged: it reads `TIK_ROOT`, `TIK_KEY`, `TIK_PQ_KEY` and `TIK_ACTOR`
from the environment as before.

```clojure
{:stores {:metio {:root "~/git/github.com/metio/.tik" :org "metio" :actor "claude"
                  :key {:command ["pasejo" "secret" "show" "tik/metio/claude"]}
                  :mcp-token-file "~/.config/tik/mcp-token-metio"}
          :personal {:root "~/git/.tik" :org "default" :actor "claude"
                     :key {:credential "tik-default-key"}}}
 :serve {:host "127.0.0.1" :port 7777}
 :notify {:poll "PT2S"}
 :pipelines [{:id :github-metio :store :metio :every "PT10M"
              :config "github.edn" :run ["bridge" "github"]}]}
```

1. **A thread-bound store context.** `tik.context/*store*` holds `{:name
   :root :key :actor}` and is bound around everything done for one store.
   `tik.cli-core/root`, `signing-key`, `pq-signing-key`, `tik.args/actor`
   and the MCP server's actor and signer read it through
   `tik.context/env` before the environment, and inside a context they
   never read the environment at all. The binding is per thread, so two
   requests for two stores running at once each see their own; futures
   carry it along. `tik.cli-core/*root*`, which the notifier binds, was
   not enough on its own, because it names only the root, and the key
   and actor would still have come from a process-wide variable.
   Rejected: one process per store behind a proxy (the maintainer asked
   for one process, and it would only move the routing); passing the
   store as an argument through every verb (hundreds of call sites, each
   a place to forget it).

2. **No guessing in a multi-store process.** Once the stores have opened,
   `tik.context/strict!` makes a read of a store variable outside any
   context throw, so a code path that forgot to bind a store fails
   instead of discovering a store from the working directory or signing
   with an inherited key. The backend also refuses to start while any of
   `TIK_ROOT`, `TIK_KEY`, `TIK_PQ_KEY` or `TIK_ACTOR` is set in its
   environment. Inside a context, `--key` naming any file but the store's
   own is refused, and a multi-store pipeline may not pass `--key` or
   `--actor` at all.

3. **Keys resolved once, at start, into a private runtime directory.** A
   store's `:key` is a path, `{:file …}`, `{:credential …}` (systemd
   `LoadCredential=`) or `{:command …}`, whose whole output is written to
   a `rw-------` file in a fresh `rwx------` directory below
   `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, removed on exit (`tik.secret/materialize-file`).
   `{:env …}` is refused, because a key in a variable is inherited by
   every child. No message carries a key: a failing command is reported
   with its stderr, a file that is not a key as "not an OpenSSH private
   key". Holding the key only in memory was declined because signing
   shells out to `ssh-keygen -Y sign -f`, which needs a file, and the
   in-process reader verifies but does not sign.

4. **Each key is proven against its own store before anything runs.**
   The backend signs a challenge with each store's key in the event
   namespace and verifies it against that store's `actors` file for that
   store's actor, exactly as an event would be verified. A key the store
   does not grant to its actor, or a store without an `actors` file,
   refuses the backend. Two stores whose keys are the same but whose
   `:org` differs are refused unless `:allow-shared-keys` names the pair,
   so one organisation's key never signs another's store by accident.
   The same holds for a pipeline's `:as` and its optional own `:key`: the
   signer must be granted to `:as` in the pipeline's store.

5. **Routing: one path per store, and a token that opens one store.**
   The board answers at `/s/<store>/`, `/s/<store>/tickets.edn` and
   `/s/<store>/explain/<id>.edn`; MCP at `/s/<store>/mcp`. Each store has
   its own token file, refused when shorter than 32 characters or
   readable by group or others, and two stores may not share one. The
   request is checked against the token of the store its path names, so
   a token sent to another store's path is a 401. Both were taken, rather
   than either alone: a token that maps to a store but shares one
   endpoint would make the store depend on which token arrived, and paths
   with one shared token would let anyone holding it reach every store.
   `/` and `/mcp` answer 404. The rebinding guard (421 for a foreign
   Host) runs before routing.

6. **Fail closed at start, isolate at run time.** A config problem, a
   store that will not open, a key that does not prove, or a token that
   does not pass refuses the whole backend, and every problem is listed
   at once. Starting the healthy stores and skipping the broken one was
   declined: the service would show as running while one store's
   bridges never sweep and its MCP answers 404, and an agent or operator
   reading "active" would take that store's silence for an empty inbox.
   A start-time failure is deterministic and fixed by editing the
   config, so refusing costs one restart. Once running, failures stay
   isolated as before: a failing pipeline logs and the others carry on,
   and a request that fails answers 500 for that request only.

7. **The notifier is reused.** `:notify` takes the settings of a
   `notify.edn` without `:stores`, and the backend runs
   `tik.notifier/notify-forever!` over its own stores' roots
   (`config-from`). The notifier binds `*root*` per store as it did and
   signs nothing, so it runs outside every store context.

8. **Per-root caches.** The derived-row cache (`tik.cli-core/cache-state`)
   is keyed by store root. It used to be one process-wide map, so a
   process deriving two stores in turn, which the notifier already did,
   flushed one store's rows, titles included, into the other store's
   `.derived-cache.json`.

## Consequences

- Probes and rollout scopes started for a store get that store's
  `TIK_ROOT`, `TIK_KEY` and `TIK_ACTOR` (`tik.context/child-env`), never
  the process's.
- MCP calls on all stores still run one at a time, behind the lock the
